messages.subject: [S] Information on S-News
messages.body_plain:
INFORMATION ON S-NEWS

Please save this information for future reference, especially to
modify your subscription or unsubscribe in the future.

The full introduction message contains additional information on the
following topics.

1. S-news objectives and appropriate use.
2. S-news addresses and subscriptions.
3. To unsubscribe...
4. Replying to messages on S-news.
5. General guidelines for posting to S-news.
6. S-news archives.
7. Mail exploders.
8. Who maintains the s-news list?
9. What should I do if I have questions or comments about list policies or
        management?  (The "s-news-advisory" list.)
10. Features of the Washington University list server.
11. Important list management commands.

To obtain the full message, send a message to

           s-news-request at wubios.wustl.edu

containing the single line in the BODY of the message:

           intro s-news

or point your Web browser at:

           http://www.biostat.wustl.edu/s-news/s-news-intro.html
-----------------------------------------------------------

TO UNSUBSCRIBE

Use one of the following forms, sent in the BODY of a
message to
           s-news-request at wubios.wustl.edu
referring to the appropriate list (regular delivery or daily digest),
and including the address you are subscribed under only if it is different
from your current mailing address.

                     unsubscribe s-news
                     unsubscribe s-news myname at my.address
                     unsubscribe s-news-digest
                     unsubscribe s-news-digest myname at my.address
-----------------------------------------------------------

S-NEWS OBJECTIVES AND APPROPRIATE USE

S-news is the discussion group on the S and S-plus systems for
statistics, graphics, and programming.  Appropriate topics must be
related to S/S-plus, including programming and usage questions and
suggestions, problem reports, and announcements of new software
(contributed and commercial), books and articles, and conferences and
educational events.  Short job announcements are also acceptable.  Long
advertisements and commercial messages that are not specifically relevant
to S/S-plus are not acceptable.
-----------------------------------------------------------

S-NEWS ADDRESSES

Mail for posting to the S-news list should be sent to:

     s-news at wubios.wustl.edu

All subscription and unsubscription requests and other list management
commands should be sent to

     s-news-request at wubios.wustl.edu

Messages that require human intervention should be sent to

     s-news-owner at wubios.wustl.edu

but you should make use of the automatic list processor commands whenever
they cover the situation.
-----------------------------------------------------------

IMPORTANT LIST MANAGEMENT COMMANDS

All Majordomo list management commands should be sent to
s-news-request at wubios.wustl.edu.  The command (or multiple commands)
should be in the body of the message, not in the subject line.  If your
mailer puts a signature at the end of the message, put the command
           end
after your list commands so the signature is not interpreted as
commands.  NEVER send commands to s-news!  (NEVER!)

A full list of Majordomo commands can be obtained by sending the command
           help

To subscribe to the list, send the command
           subscribe s-news
or for the digest version,
           subscribe s-news-digest
You will be sent a confirmation message to which you must reply to make
sure that you actually desired to subscribe.  This is intended to prevent
forged subscriptions.  Note that subscriptions to the immediate-delivery
and digest versions are handled like two separate lists, so if you want to
switch from immediate delivery to digest, you must unsubscribe to s-news
and subscribe to s-news-digest.

If you want to subscribe using a different address than the one you are
sending from, use the command
           subscribe s-news myname at my.address

To unsubscribe, send one of the following commands as appropriate:
           unsubscribe s-news
           unsubscribe s-news-digest
           unsubscribe s-news myname at my.address
           unsubscribe s-news-digest myname at my.address

messages.subject: [S] predict.lm vs predict.gam
messages.body_plain:
Hi S users,

This may well be an old issue or even a FAQ - however:

For the use of predict.lm, there are warnings, e.g., Chambers & Hastie page
108, V & R, 2nd ed. page 209 to the affect, as I understand it, predict.lm
will not work correctly if any of the new variables are functionally
"derived" from the old variables. Derived here means estimated from
(mean(x)) as opposed to say x^2.

predict.gam is the suggested recourse.

I have been toying with a base data frame, say data for y=f(xo), xo is an
arbitrary matrix, f is a linear sum, and deriving other x matrices, xi, to
compare how misc. routines behave on the modified data. Things such as

x1 <- xo + rnorm(N,m,s)
x2 <- cbind(xo[,1] + n1, xo[,2] + n2, ...) string of numbers to impose
shifts on the data columns)
x3 <- combinations/variations of x1, x2

I then make a lm(xo) or gam(linear sum of the xo cols) and use predict.lm
or predict.gam on the xi.

No matter what values I use for m,s in rnorm() or shift numbers, lm returns
the identical, nearly exact, result for y and with standard errors that
never change.

predict.gam on the other hand returns what I would expect, as the modified
xi depart further from xo, the returned y values have increasing errors.

What am I missing, or is something strange here?

John

John Fennick

Blacksburg, VA 24060
USA

Fax (540) 552-0261 (Tel first for setup)

messages.subject: [S] Position Announcement
messages.body_plain:
UNIVERSITY OF COLORADO-DENVER 
                 DEPARTMENT OF MATHEMATICS 
  
 The Department of Mathematics at the University of Colorado at Denver 
 seeks to fill a tenure-track position at the Assistant Professor level,
 beginning August 2000.  Higher rank is possible, contingent on budgetary
 approval.  We offer B.S., M.S., and Ph.D. degrees; faculty interests 
 span computational mathematics, discrete mathematics, engineering 
 mathematics, operations research, probability, and statistics.  We seek 
 qualified applicants in statistics and prefer someone who can interface 
 with faculty in other areas.  
  
 Applicants are expected to show strong potential for research and 
 teaching and have a commitment to professional service.  Applicants 
 must have, or expect to receive by next August, a Ph.D. in statistics or 
 a related discipline.   The Department currently maintains a network of
 Unix- and Linux-based computers, with S-Plus being the principal 
 statistics environment.
  
 We will begin screening applications January 10, 2000.  
 To apply, please send a current vita, list of publications, a statement 
 of research plans and goals, a statement of teaching philosophy, 
 and arrange to have three letters of recommendation sent to: 
  
     Search Committee 
     Mathematics Department - Campus Box 170 
     University of Colorado at Denver 
     P.O. Box 173364 
     Denver, CO 80217-3364 
     Fax: 303-556-8550 
  
 CU-Denver is located in the heart of downtown Denver, 1/2 block 
 off Larimer Square, close to LoDo and the Denver Performing Arts 
 Center, and 70 miles from Keystone, Vail, and other ski resorts. 
 For more information on our department and the university, please 
 visit our web site at http://www-math.cudenver.edu.  
  
 The University of Colorado at Denver is an equal opportunity 
 employer committed to excellence through inclusiveness.  The Colorado 
 Open Records Act (C.R.S. 24-72-204) requires a written request 
 for confidentiality at the time of application.  Applications without 
 such a request may be open records and may be disclosed.

KDD-2000 Call for Panel Proposals

                            KDD-2000: 
             The Sixth ACM SIGKDD International Conference
               on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining

                 August 20-23, 2000, Boston, MA, USA

                 http://www.acm.org/sigkdd/kdd2000

                     Call for Panel Proposals
    http://www.acm.org/sigs/sigkdd/kdd2000/KDD2000-PanelsCFP.htm

           Panel proposals due:    March 3, 2000
           Expected notification:  April 10, 2000

     KDD-2000 Panels Chair:  Alex Tuzhilin, New York University,
                             (atuzhili at stern.nyu.edu)

The Sixth International Conference on Knowledge Discovery and Data
Mining (KDD-2000) is the premiere event for the data mining community
expected to bring together more than 800 attendees from academia and
industry. Among other activities, the conference program includes panels,
and the Program Committee invites submission of proposals for the panels to
be held at the conference.

Panel proposals are expected to address new, exciting, and controversial
issues. They should include a summary of the topics to be covered, names and
affiliations of up to 4 panelists who have made a commitment to participate,
a short summary of their position statements, and a brief biography of each
participant. A mix of industry and academic panel members is encouraged.

Panel proposals should be submitted electronically in the ASCII format to
the Panel Chair Alex Tuzhilin (atuzhili at stern.nyu.edu) by March 3, 2000. The
expected notification date is April 10, 2000.

messages.subject_clean: [S] lme and gls: Function for extracting Least-squares means?
messages.body_plain:
Hello to all my friends in the stats world, who did not know I was on
this list (my first posting).

Before I re-invent the wheel, does anyone have a function that
calculates the least-squares means (adj.means) for factor terms in the
fixed effects part of a mixed effects model for gls and/or lme objects?
That is the results from a mixed effects linear model. 

For instance there is no model.tables.lme function in nlme3.2, like the
model.tables.anova.

I'd be quite happy with simply an equivalent of the model.means.lm
function.

Thanks,

James

new on-line user resources, training opportunities and 
acadmeic licensing schemes.

The roadshow will focus on introducing S-PLUS 2000 for Windows to
new and potential S-PLUS users but may also be of interest to

messages.subject: [S] Statistical Software Prize
messages.body_plain:
Dear colleagues:

This summer, the ASA will award a new prize for statistical software.
This note is to encourage you to apply or nudge someone you know to
apply.

The award is for software that contributes to better use of computing
in statistical research and applications, written while the applicant
was a student.  There is a $1,000 prize plus the opportunity to give
an invited talk at the Joint Statistical Meetings.

The goal of the prize is to recognize software contributions that make
our use of the computer better.  This is interpreted broadly, so both
directly "statistical" contributions and other improvements in the
computing environment are eligible.  We want to recognize the good
work done in this area and to encourage students to contribute in the
future.

The work should have been done while the applicant was a student.  It
is not necessary that the applicant still be a student, and there is
no restriction on the level or the area of study.

In this first year of the prize, particularly, we are anxious to
encourage wide participation.

The prize originated from the ACM's Software System award which I
received in May, 1999; the money from that award was used to endow the
new prize (which is why my name is attached to it).  The ACM award was
a recognition by the computing profession of the contributions
statistical software has made, and so I hope the new prize will reward
and encourage such contributions.

Applications should go to Lionel Galway:

        Chambers Software Award
        c/o Lionel Galway
        The RAND Corporation
        1700 Main St.
        Santa Monica, CA 90407
        Lionel_Galway at rand.org

The announcement, with details of the requirements, is on my web site
(http://www.cs.bell-labs.com/~jmc/asaAward.html) and more information
is available from the ASA Computing Section web site
(http://www-stat.montclair.edu/asascs/).

The deadline for applications is February 24, so please act now!

Regards,
 John Chambers

-- 
John M. Chambers                  jmc at bell-labs.com
Bell Labs, Lucent Technologies    office: (908)582-2681
700 Mountain Avenue, Room 2C-282  fax:    (908)582-3340
Murray Hill, NJ  07974            web: http://www.cs.bell-labs.com/~jmc

messages.subject: [S] graphsheet differs in release 1 and 2 of S-Plus 2000
messages.subject_clean: [S] graphsheet differs in release 1 and 2 of S-Plus 2000
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-users,
I have created some standard plotting functions. One feature is that the
plots always 
come out (on paper) with the exact same size. These functions were developed
under
S-Plus 4.5, and worked fine under S-Plus 2000 Release 1 (July 1, 1999).
However, under
S-Plus 2000 Release 2 (November 1, 1999) they have a new size! It therefore
appears that 
the size of the graphsheet device has changed from release 1 to 2. 

To check this I reinstalled S-Plus 2000 R1 on my Windows NT (pentium 3)
computer, and
asked for the (default) absolute device size using par("din"). Thereafter I
updated the 
installation to release 2 and did the same thing. The results show that
indeed 
something has changed:

par("din") gives: 

  11.363244  7.938046 for Release 1 and

  10.67033  8.17033 for Release 2.

The above results go for a "clean machine" where par("din") is the first
command when S-plus 
wakes up. If I explicitly invoke graphsheet(), I get the same results. For
win.graph, however, 
there is no difference between release 1 and 2. Another observation: If I
make a printout of 
show.settings() or any other graph, the sizes I get on paper differ from
release 1 and 2. I print 
using the menu: File|Print graph sheet.

To get my old "standard" plots to come out the right way under release 2, I
now do the following:
Before I make a command-line plot with traditional graphics I issue:

   graphsheet(width=11.6929135, height=8.267716)

this approximately returns the din-values to those in release 1. When I want
a trellis graph, I write:

   trellis.device(device=graphsheet, width=11.6929135, height=8.267716)

I do not know what happens for the editable graphics (based on Auxum). Now
my question: 
Is there a better (more permanent) way to redefine the size of a graphsheet?

Finally, I would like to say that this little problem took me quite some
time to identify. I thought 
something was wrong with the parameters in par or that the function with my
standard graph had been
messed up. I do not understand why such a fundamental feature as the size of
a device can suddenly 
change from one release to another?

- Claus

>

That is not the definition in use, which is certainly confusing. You need
to use selectMethod to see what plot does as a new-style generic.

> > lines  # Method selection fails
> function(x, y, ...)
> .Call("S_c_use_method", "lines")
>

No! First, you don't own them and second it would have widespread
consequences.

I don't fully understand your example, but the recommended way is to set a
method (new-style) for xyCall, which will then be used by lines (and plot
unless you have a more specific one). I think that is the key to getting
lines to work.

messages.subject: [S] Summary: track CPU time in simulation
messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: track CPU time in simulation
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Thanks to everyone who replied my message. It turns out that the question
is trivial. Most people suggested use 'unix.time' , 'dos.time' or
'proc.time' as in Prof. Ripley's message(attached below).  I also attach
few other answers below .

My original query:
"I have a question that may be trivial to you. 
I am running some simulations on both PC(window NT) Splus2000 and
unix/linux Splus5.1. I would like to know the actual CPU time spent on
the simulations. How can I do this? Thanks for your help."

*****************************************************************************
1. From Prof. Brian D Ripley:

You can time by dos.time on 2000 (elapsed time) and unix.time on 5.1,
or call proc.time and difference on either.

As far as I know there is no way to get CPU (rather than elapsed) time on
2000, probably as there is no way to get it (portably) on Windows 9x. It is
possible on NT, and it would be useful to have it (hint to MathSoft).

******************************************************************************
2. From: james.holtman at convergys.com

Here is a function that I 'sprinkle' throughout my code to track both the
CPU and memory usage:

 my.stats <- function(text = "stats")
{
    cat(text, "-", sys.call(sys.parent())[1], ": ", proc.time(), " : ",
round(
        memory.size()/2^20, 1), "MB\n")
}

This lists out the function name that it was called from, the CPU time
(proctime) and memory used.

Hope this helps
******************************************************************************
3. From: "Peter Alspach" <palspach at hort.cri.nz>

Try

my.time(your.function)

where 

my.time <- function(expr)
{
#  my.time function from SPlus 3 Programmer's Manual p2-61, 
#  with modifications for version 4.5 (mem.tally.reset() &
mem.tally.report()).
        mem.tally.reset()
        l <- sys.parent(1)
        if(l == 1)
                l <- F
        on.exit(cat("Timing stopped at:", proc.time() - time, 
                "\n"))
        time <- proc.time()
        eval(expr, local = l)
        new.time <- proc.time()
        on.exit()
        if(length(new.time) == 3)
                new.time <- c(new.time, 0, 0)
        if(length(time) == 3)
                time <- c(time, 0, 0)
        val <- new.time - time
        attr(val, "Memory tally") <- mem.tally.report()
        val
}

The question is asked: why do the coefficients change so much with a
slight change in the data?

'statistical' sample size is the number of events, not the number of subjects
or observations.  The first coef was 12.7 with a standard error of 10.7,
which changed to -0.2 in the second run.  With a tiny data set, a change of
just over 1 SE due to a data modification is not surprizing, whatever the
model being used.  For 2 covariates on 6 points I might have expected worse.

messages.body_plain:
Dear S+ users,

Please forgive me if this seems like a very basic question, but this is my
first look at mixed-effect models.  I've searched all my limited resources
(S+ manuals, Venables and Ripley (1999), and the StatLib archives), and
can't quite find the answer to my question.  I'm using S-plus 2000 Release 2
on a PC running Windows95.  Basically, I'm trying to figure out if S+ is
doing what I think/hope it's doing, and that it's actually the correct thing
to do.

I'm trying to estimate an equation to predict the success rate of elk
hunters in Idaho.  The state is broken up into about 20 units, and I have
data for each of these units for 6 years.  My dependent variable is the
success rate of hunters in each of the units in each year.  Some of the
independent variables that may be related to the success rate change across
the years and differ between units (e.g. length of the hunting season that
year, what weapons were allowed that year, an estimate of the elk population
size that year, etc).  There are other independent variables that describe
the physical features of each unit that do not change over time (at least at
the scale which I'm able to measure them), such as road density, percent
area that is forested, etc. As such, my data looks a bit like this (but with
more years, more units, and more variables...these are made-up numbers):

Unit    Year    Success Season_Length   Elk_Population_Size     Road_Density
1       1990    0.2             100             1000            0.05
1       1991    0.15            120             1020            0.05
1       1992    0.18            110             900             0.05
2       1990    0.1             60              200             0.02
2       1991    0.09            60              250             0.02
2       1992    0.15            80              220             0.02

What I am trying to do is determine which variables should be included, and
estimate the parameters for the equations :

S(i,j) = b0 + b1(j) + b2*Season_Length(i,j) + b3*Pop_Size(i,j)... (eq 1)
b1(j) = a0(j) + a1*Road_Density(j) + a2*Percent_Forested_Area(j) + .... (eq
2)

Where S(i,j) is the properly transformed success rate in year i for unit j.
Basically, the variable that allows each unit to have a separate intercept,
b1(j), is a function of the attributes of the unit (which do not change over
time).  

To test this, what I think I would use would be the lme() equation as such:

lme(Success ~ Season_Length, random = ~1|Unit, data = my_data_file)

This particular equation would allow me to test the significance of
Season_Length, and produce estimates for the parameters b0, a0(j) and b2.
This makes sense to me, and I think it's what I'm trying to do and supposed
to do (But I could easily be wrong).

Where I get confused is when I'm trying to test for the significance of
something like Road_Density which is a continuous-valued, constant attribute
of the Unit.  From what I've been able to decipher so far, I should use the
command:

lme(Success ~ Road_Density, random = ~Road_Density|Unit, data =
my_data_file)

if I want to allow the parameter for Road_Density to vary by Unit, and the
command:

lme(Success ~ Road_Density, random = ~1|Unit, data = my_data_file)

to test whether the parameter is the same for all Units. What I can't quite
figure out is how S+ takes into account the fact that Road_Density is
constant over time, or whether it explicitly needs to.  For instance if this
were a repeated measures anova (using the aov() statement with
"+Error(Unit)" included), there are separate tests for within Units and
between Units, each with the appropriate degrees of freedom.  Does the
mixed-effect model simply take both of those into account and produce an
over-all significance test? 

Is this making any sense?  Am I interpreting all this properly?  Any
thoughts on whether this is really what I should be doing?

Thank you for your help!!!!

Sincerely,
Andy

messages.body_plain:
James Roger wrote:

>I posted the following query:
>"Before I re-invent the wheel, does anyone have a function that
>calculates the least-squares means (adj.means) for factor terms in the
>fixed effects part of a mixed effects model for gls and/or lme objects?
>That is the results from a mixed effects linear model. 
>
>For instance there is no model.tables.lme function in nlme3.2, like the
>model.tables.anova."
>CONCLUSION:
....
>I am still waiting. I will only summarize again if something positive
>comes up.

Also, model.tables() appears dangerous.  It requires a warning
that it gives meaningful output only for a limited class of models
(Which class?)

The following is a balanced incomplete block design.

> options(contrasts=c("contr.treatment","contr.poly"), digits=4)
> bdes
  trt blk   y 
1   a   A 0.4
6   c   A 1.2
2   a   B 0.6
3   b   B 1.0
4   b   C 2.0
5   c   C 3.0
> bdes.aov<-aov(y~blk+trt,data=bdes)
> coef(bdes.aov)
 (Intercept) blkB blkC trtb trtc 
         0.3  0.4  1.6  0.2    1
> tapply(bdes$y,bdes$trt,mean)  # Calculate marginal means.
   a   b   c 
 0.5 1.5 2.1
> model.tables(bdes.aov)

Tables of effects

 blk 
        A        B      C 
 -0.56667 -0.56667 1.1333

 trt 
    a     b    c 
 -0.3 -0.15 0.45
Warning messages:
  Model was refit to allow projection in: model.tables.aov(bdes.aov)
> 

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
One might have expected the `c' minus `a' contrast to be 1.  
model.tables makes this 0.75

Nor is model.tables() calculating the marginal mean of the 
observed values, or of the fitted values.  (Because of the 
balance in this design, these are the same as the marginal 
means of the observed values.)

So there should surely be a warning that model.tables can be 
relied on only when each treatment is present equally often 
at levels of other factors, i. e. only for complete designs.

messages.subject: [S] coxph with time interaction (follow-up)
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

Yesterday I asked a question about somewhat strange results in a time by
covariate interaction in a Cox model:
results changed a lot with a slight change in the data.
I received two reactions:

-------------------------------------------------------
Ken Hess:
You don't say how you create the dataset, but assuming that you are doing
it correctly, the remaining question seems to be how fine the regular grid
is relative to the actual event times. If the grid is much "rougher" than
the original event times, then this could create the difference in the
results. I have used both grids formed by the original times and from
subsets of these and have gotten similar results. We have an S+ function
for generating the new dataframe from an existing dataframe.
---------------------------------------------------------
Terry Therneau:
  There are n=6 total events in the data set.  For a cox model, the 
'statistical' sample size is the number of events, not the number of
subjects
or observations.  The first coef was 12.7 with a standard error of 10.7,
which changed to -0.2 in the second run.  With a tiny data set, a change of
just over 1 SE due to a data modification is not surprizing, whatever the
model being used.  For 2 covariates on 6 points I might have expected worse.
----------------------------------------------------------

I created the data set via the function "expand.breakpoints", as posted to
s-news by John MainDonald on Nov 23, 1998.
What I forgot to say in my original message is that I obtained similar
results in a much larger data set: 222 cases with 130 events.
The data set I supplied served only as an illustration.
Here are my original results (Data1: coarse grid; Data2: grid based on event
times):
coxph(formula = Surv(Tstart, Tstop, stat) ~ cd4 + cd4:I(Tstop - 5), data =
Data1, na.action = na.omit)

                   coef exp(coef) se(coef)      z       p 
             cd4 -0.322     0.725   0.3237 -0.995 0.32000
cd4:I(Tstop - 5) -0.293     0.746   0.0857 -3.416 0.00064

Likelihood ratio test=57.6  on 2 df, p=3.08e-013  n= 4002 
-----------
coxph(formula = Surv(Tstart, Tstop, stat) ~ cd4 + cd4:I(Tstop - 5), data =
Data2, na.action = na.omit)

                  coef exp(coef) se(coef)     z        p 
             cd4 -1.76     0.172   0.2791 -6.32 2.7e-010
cd4:I(Tstop - 5)  0.19     1.209   0.0778  2.44 1.5e-002

Likelihood ratio test=51.2  on 2 df, p=7.51e-012  n= 16901 
-------------
On the other hand, with Tstart instead of Tstop, results are more or less
equal:
coxph(formula = Surv(Tstart, Tstop, stat) ~ cd4 + cd4:I(Tstart - 5), data =
Data1, na.action = na.omit)

                    coef exp(coef) se(coef)     z        p 
              cd4 -1.749     0.174   0.2731 -6.40 1.5e-010
cd4:I(Tstart - 5)  0.192     1.212   0.0782  2.46 1.4e-002

Likelihood ratio test=51.3  on 2 df, p=7.1e-012  n= 4002 
-------------
coxph(formula = Surv(Tstart, Tstop, stat) ~ cd4 + cd4:I(Tstart - 5), data =
Data2, na.action = na.omit)

                    coef exp(coef) se(coef)     z        p 
              cd4 -1.759     0.172   0.2771 -6.35 2.2e-010
cd4:I(Tstart - 5)  0.192     1.212   0.0787  2.45 1.4e-002

Likelihood ratio test=51.3  on 2 df, p=7.34e-012  n= 16901 

Greetings,
Ronald Geskus

> very

>

> with

> 
> As I intend to apply cross-validation procedures to select good values for
> the

> predictors

messages.subject: [S] Calling nls() from apply()
messages.body_plain:
I have a question about calling nls() from apply(),
but it may be related to not understanding how values 
are passed from apply() to any function.  I've "solved"
the problem, but I don't know why.

 The objective is to fit parameters to a simple
nonlinear model, y = b[0]*x^b[1], where the parameters
b[0] and b[1] are to be estimated.  The same model is 
fit repeatedly to many data sets, say B.

 I used to apply() function to do the estimation:

ests <- apply(matrix(1:B,B,1),1,custom.nls,y=sim.number,x=sim.diam,
              mystart=dens.start)

 where
  sim.number is a B by n matrix of responses, y, with
            each row being a particular data set.  
  sim.diam is a B by n matrix of the predictor variable, x,
            with each row being a data set.
  dens.start is a vector of initial values for b[0] and b[1]

and nls is being called from the function custom.nls.  

 The original version of custom.nls was:

custom.nls <- function(rownumber,y,x,mystart) {
 out <- coef(nls(y[rownumber,] ~ b0*x[rownumber,]^b1,
         control=list(maxiter=100),start=mystart))
 return(out)
}

when this was called by apply(), the following error message resulted:

> apply(matrix(1:B,B,1),1,custom.nls,y=sim.number,x=sim.diam,
  +   mystart=dens.start)
Error in nls(y[rownumber,  ] ~ b0 * x[rownumber,  ..: Object "..1" not found
Dumped
Error was while calling subroutine "setup_nonlin"

 The error went away when custom.nls was revised to:

custom.nls <- function(rownumber,y,x,mystart) {
 yr <- y[rownumber,]
 xr <- x[rownumber,]
 out <- coef(nls(yr ~ b0*xr^b1,control=list(maxiter=100),start=mystart))
 return(out)
}

and the resulting estimates were correct (based on doing one row
at a time "manually").

 In the course of trying to debug the first version, some simple
cat() statements were used to see if the right values were being
passed to custom.nls().  "Strangely" enough the first version worked.

custom.nls <- function(rownumber,y,x,mystart) {
  cat("row=",rownumber,"\n")
  cat("start=",mystart,"\n")
  cat("y=",y[rownumber,],"\n")
  cat("x=",x[rownumber,],"\n")
  out <- coef(nls(y[rownumber,] ~ b0*x[rownumber,]^b1,
         control=list(maxiter=100),start=mystart))
 return(out)
}

  Any ideas as to what's going on?  

Ken Newman
Division of Statistics
University of Idaho

messages.subject: [S] RE: graphsheet differs in release 1 and 2 of S-Plus 2000 (solution)
messages.subject_clean: [S] RE: graphsheet differs in release 1 and 2 of S-Plus 2000 (solution)
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-plus 2000 users,
On January 5, I reported to this list, that plots created with the
graphsheet device come out in different sizes under S-plus 2000 Release 1
and Release 2. I now think, I know what is going on. 

[1] What has changed? 
The (factory) default settings in S-plus 2000 R1 (and I believe this also
goes for version 4.5) was: 

  PageWidth = "printer"
  PageHeight = "printer"

If the printer (as in my case) uses A4 paper, then the width and height will
be set accordingly. Likewise, if the printer is set to US letter paper. Now,
in S-plus 2000 R2, Mathsoft has changed the graphsheet (factory) defaults
to:

  PageWidth = "11"
  PageHeight = "8.5"

Which corresponds to the US letter paper size. Always! Therefore, these
changes in (factory) defaults affect me (and I guess also many other users
with A4 printers). If the printer anyway uses US letter paper, then the
change in graphsheet defaults should have no impact. 

[2] What is the "solution"?
To permanently return the page size defaults to those of Release 1 (or
something else), I simply use the command:

   guiModifyDefaults("GraphSheet",
        PageOrientation = "Landscape",
        Units = "INCH",
        PageWidth = "printer",
        PageHeight = "printer")

This can also be done by right-clicking on the plot and use the layout menu
item. Thereafter right-click again on the plot and select the item: "Save
Graph Sheet as default".  For completeness, I repeat, that to return to A4
in single plots I use, 

  graphsheet(width=11.6929135, height=8.267716)  or 
  trellis.device(device=graphsheet, width=11.6929135, height=8.267716)

The numbers are the standard A4 210 mm x 297 mm size in units of inches (1
in = 25.4 mm). Finally, I would like to thank Frank E Harrell Jr, Brian D
Ripley, and Frank Biedermann for useful responses regarding the above
matters. 

- Claus

messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Andrew Sinclair Alan Zaslavsky Tom Burr Samuel Buttrey Charles
Berry Bill Venables and Brian Ripley for their quick responses.

The original message was:

> Hi,
>
> I am generating a vector of binary variables x. We observe y which
satisfies
> Pr[y=1|x=1]=theta and Pr[y=0|x=0]=eta. This is done with
>
>     n  <- 10^4
>     px <- 1/10
>     x  <- rbinom(n,1,px)
>     xs <- unlist(lapply(x,missC,theta,eta))
>
>
>     missC <- function(x,theta=90/100,eta=10/100)
>     {
>     if(x==1) rbinom(1,1,theta)
>         else
>     rbinom(1,1,1-eta)
>     }
>
> I am sure there is a faster way of doing this, can anybody help -

With responses:

rbinom(length(x), 1, ifelse(x, theta, eta))

or

runif(n)<ifelse(x,1-eta,theta)

or

n <- 10^4
px <- 1/10
x <- rbinom(n, 1, px)
py <- 1 - eta + x*(theta - 1 + eta)
xs <- rbinom(n, 1, py)

All seem to run much faster that the original.

Ori

messages.subject: [S] doubly-censored survival data
messages.body_plain:
Dear people of s-news..

Is anyone aware of whether or not the generalised form of 
Turnbull's (1976) self-consistency algorithm proposed 
has been coded in S to faciliate the analysis of doubly-censored 
survival data? The function kaplanMeier.fit in S-PLUS does not 
seem to accommodate observations that are both interval-censored
on the left and right-censored  (I say this because the
the censor.codes argument of kaplanMeier.fit appears to
be limited to only one of four censoring states - not
two).

I have coded the algorithm proposed by De Gruttola and
Lagakos (1989) for the analysis of such doubly-censored
data in S.  I would be most interested to learn of whether others have 
tackled this problem before in S as I would value some benchmark to
compare my work to.  I am happy to to exchange or share 
my code with others.  

Later work has incorporated the presence of a covariate in the 
analysis of doubly-censored survival data.  It might be useful to 
develop such a function in S if it does not already exist?

Daniel

messages.subject: Re: [S] "Copula"
messages.body_plain:
> 
> Hi, everybody:
> Can anybody give a brief explanation and/or give some reference on "Copula"
> method in bivariate simulation?

> (Who is "copula", what is "copula", who to apply "copula", how to correctly
> spell "copula", is it good or bad, etc??) 

This idea is gaining more attention than I would have thought it
was really worth so perhaps we (ie mainly I) should be a bit more
aware of it.

If you take any univariate random variable X with continuous
distribution function F(x) then it is well known that Y = F(X)
[watch the capitals!] has a Uniform(0, 1) distribution.  Easy.

OK, now take any p-dimensional continuous distribution with
coordinate random variables X1, X2, ..., Xp, having (continuous)
marginal distributions F1(x), ... Fp(x).  Define Y1 = F1(X1),
..., Yp = Fp(Xp).  Then (Y1, ..., Yp) has a continuous
multivariate distribution with uniform marginals and such a
distribution is given the (mildly suggestive?) name of copula.
Why? dunno.

The contention is that the dependency relations between the Xi's
must be completely summarized in a canonical way by the copula,
so a modelling strategy you might consider is to think about how
the cupola should look first and then think separately about the
marginal distributions of the coordinates.  This is very similar
to thinking about how the correlation matrix should look first in
multivariate normal modelling and then thinking separately about
the variances and the means.  One strategy, but only one.

It is the strongly coordinate dependent aspect of the cupola that
I find a bit limiting.  Also, in modelling multivariate
distributions I find other strategies are often more natural: for
example think about the marginal distribution of one variable
first and the conditional distribution of a second given the
first, a third given the first two, and so on (also a strongly
coordinate-dependent strategy, of course!).  I have seen books
that implicitly suggest that copulas are the royal road to
multivariate modelling but I think you still need many tools in
your modelling (and simulation) armory.

To inject a little S relevance, it would nevertheless be good if
some of the newer modelling and simulation tools based on copula
ideas were to find their way into S-PLUS, as until they are used
in practice fairly extensively their true value will not really
become apparent.  Does anyone have any contributions to make?

Bill Venables.
--

messages.subject: Re: [S] "Copula" (long)
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

> 
> Date: Wed, 12 Jan 2000 09:39:58 +1000
> From: Bill Venables <William.Venables at cmis.CSIRO.AU>
> Subject: Re: [S] "Copula" 
> 
> ...
>
> The contention is that the dependency relations between the Xi's
> must be completely summarized in a canonical way by the copula,
> so a modelling strategy you might consider is to think about how
> the cupola should look first and then think separately about the
> marginal distributions of the coordinates.  This is very similar
> to thinking about how the correlation matrix should look first in
> multivariate normal modelling and then thinking separately about
> the variances and the means.  

One possible application of copulas is in finance
where clients often have strong views about the 
distribution of returns (daily changes in prices)
for a individual market (e.g. US equities)
but are less clear about the dependencies between
markets (e.g. US equity v Australian equities).

Typically correlation is used to measure this dependency
which implies a multi-variate Gaussian world.
In reality, returns are often non-Gaussian 
(e.g. fat-tailed or skewed).
In addition, some markets have the characteristic that
they will all fall together (strong dependency) 
but they rise more independently (weaker dependency)
so there is a kind of asymmetry in the dependency relationship.
In addition, the bigger the fall the more likely it
is that other markets will also suffer big falls.

The main potential advantage of copulas for me
is the seperation between marginals and the dependency
because (in finance) the former are often understood and modelled
in detail but dependency is almost always interpreted as 
meaning Pearson's correlation, which isnt always appropriate.
Any alternative approaches to dependency are to be welcomed.

That said, I think there is still a lot of work to be done
before copulas become more widely used.
How do you decide which copula to use and 
how do you fit the dependency parameter to observed data?

> To inject a little S relevance, it would nevertheless be good if
> some of the newer modelling and simulation tools based on copula
> ideas were to find their way into S-PLUS, as until they are used
> in practice fairly extensively their true value will not really
> become apparent.  Does anyone have any contributions to make?

I had a go at multivariate simulation using copulas based on 
Algorithm 3.3 of 
Understanding relationships using copulas, 
Edward W. Frees and Emiliano A. Valdez,
North American Actuarial Journal, 
vol 2, num 1, pp 1-25 (circa 1999?)

This seems to work for the (default) Clayton copula 
(see examples below).
Note that the function isnt working 
for the Gumbel copula 'rcopula(cop="gum")' cos
I couldnt relate the definition of a stable distribution
given in the paper to the 'rstab' function in SPlus.
I am interested in any solutions to this.

Regards,

John.

john.gavin at wdr.com

John Gavin
Quantitative Risk Models and Statistics
Warburg Dillon Read
1 Finsbury Ave (1st floor)
London EC2M 2PP, UK
Phone +44 171 567 4289
Fax   +44 171 568 5352

### the 'help' file, function and examples follow (long) 

# COPULA SIMULATION GENERATED FROM COMPOUND DISTRIBUTIONS

# k-D multivariate distn with a (Clayton-Cook-Johnston) 
# compound copula
# + easily extends to from 2-D to n-D
# - only does positive dependency (dependency > 0) 
# - a latent r.v. is required => extra 50% workload for 2-D, 
#   extra 10% workload for 10-D 

# Generate U(0,1) with properties based on a 'dependency' parameter
# The Clayton-Cook-Johnston (CCJ) copula requires a gamma distn 
# as a latent variable to link the 'k' U(0,1)s in each 
# simulated k-D vector.
# NB: the gamma shape parameter is a function of the dependency
# NB: the gamma rate parameter is defaulted to 1

# dependency  Positive real vector of dependency parameters for 
#             CCJ copula
# dist        List of SPlus distn names for marginals 
#             e.g. for a normal marginal use 'norm'
#             Each list is itself a list of the parameters 
#             for that function.
#             e.g. for a N(1,2) and gamma(3,2) use 
#             'distn = list(norm=list(1,2),gamma=list(ra=2, sh =3))'
#             A character vector of distribution names is 
#             also accepted
#             e.g. distn = rep("norm", 3) to get three N0,1)s
# copula      Character vector of length 1 to idenfity copula 
#             to be used.
#             Choices are 'independent', 'clayton' or 'gumbel'
#             but ONLY 'clayton' WORKS currently.
#             Partial matching allowed.
# sizeSample  Size (i.e. number) of the marginal distribution samples.
#             A positive integer so each marginal has the same size.
# rndDep      Number of decimal places to round dependency when
#             generating a factor at the end.
#             This has no effect on the calculations.
# return value
#             A list. 
#             The simulaed data is a data.frame called '$data'.
#             This data.frame  contains k+1 columns, k-columns 
#             for the k-D data and
#             the extra column contains the dependency parameter 
#             value for that k-D vector.
#             There are sizeSample rows in the data.frame .
# bugs        Only does the Clayton copula currently. 
#             Extend to independence and gumbel
#             Only tested on SPlus 2000 R2 on NT4 SP3
#             Should (?) work in R but some examples require trellis.
# references  Algorithm 3.3 of 
#             Understanding relationships using copulas, 
#             Edward W. Frees and Emiliano A. Valdez,
#             North American Actuarial Journal, 
#             vol 2, num 1, pp 1-25 (circa 1999?)
# examples    See below.

rcopula <- function(
  dependency = 2, distn = list(norm = list(mean = 0, sd = 1) , 
  norm = list(sd = 1) ) , 
  copula = "clayton", sizeSample = 10, rndDep = 4)
{  if (   ! ( is.numeric(dependency) && length(dependency) >= 1 && 
             all ( dependency > 0) ) ) 
    stop("'dependency' must a vector of positive real number(s).")
  if (   ! ( is.numeric(sizeSample) && length(sizeSample) == 1 && 
             sizeSample > 0 ) ) 
    stop("'sizeSample' must a single positive number.")
  if (mode(distn) == "character") 
  { # e.g. distn = c("gamma") => distn = list( gamma = list() ) 
    temp      <- vector("list", length(distn))
    names(temp)   <- distn
    distn      <- temp
  } else if (any( names(distn) == "") ) 
  {  # combination of character names and lists
     temp  <- unlist(distn[names(distn) == ""] )
     distn [names(distn) == "" ] <- vector("list", 1) # vector(0)
     names(distn) [names(distn) == ""] <- temp
  }
  choices  <- c("clayton", "gumbel", 'independent')
  which.method <- pmatch(casefold(copula), choices)
  if(is.na(which.method)) 
    stop("method must be \"clayton\" or \"gumbel\" or \"indep\".")  
  copula  <- choices[which.method ]
  # check range of dependency parameter
  if ( copula == "clayton" & any ( dependency <= 0) ) 
    warning("some dependency values maybe out of range i.e. <= 0")
  if ( copula == "gumbel"  & any ( dependency <  1) ) 
    stop("Some dependency values are out of range i.e. dep < 1")
  # for each dependency value generate a latent variable 
  # whose length = sizeSample
  latentVar <- switch (copula, 
    clayton = rep( rgamma(sizeSample * length(dependency) , 
       shape = rep(1/dependency, each=sizeSample)), length(distn)), 
    # rstab for Gumbel-Hougaard copula?
    # gumbel = rep( rstab (sizeSample * length(dependency) , 
    #   index = rep(1/dependency , each = sizeSample )  , 
    #   skew = rep(0, each = sizeSample ) ) , length(distn) ) , 
    gumbel    = stop("'gumbel' not available yet"), 
    independent  = stop("'independence' not available yet"),
    stop("failed to find a switch for latenVar")
  )
  corr.full <- rep( rep(dependency, each = sizeSample) , 
    length(distn) ) 
  ClaytonAdjUnif <- function(dependency , latentVar ) 
    (  1 - log( runif( length(latentVar ) ) ) / latentVar   
    )^(-1/dependency )
  GumbelAdjUnif <- function(dependency , latentVar ) 
    exp( - ( - log( runif( length(latentVar ) ) ) / latentVar 
       )^(-1/dependency )  )
  # call ClaytonAdjUnif _once_. Pass in data ordered 
  # by dependency then by distn (each of len sizeSample)
  adj.unif  <- data.frame(
    unif = switch(copula,
      clayton    = ClaytonAdjUnif (corr.full, latentVar ), 
      gumbel      = GumbelAdjUnif  (corr.full, latentVar ), 
      stop("failed to find a switch for latenVar")
    ),
    # names(distn) might have duplicates so 
    # count over them to guarantee uniqueness
    distn.num = rep ( seq(length(distn)) , 
      each = sizeSample * length(dependency) ) 
  )
  data <- data.frame( 
    lapply(seq(length(distn)) , function(x, adj.unif, distn) 
      # names(distn) might have duplicates so count over it
      # call 'do.call' _once_ for each marginal in 'distn' 
      # regardless of number of dependencys given in 'dependency'
      do.call( paste("q", names(distn)[x] , sep="") , 
        c(p = list(adj.unif$unif[adj.unif$distn.num == x] ) , 
        distn[[x]] ) ) , adj.unif, distn) 
  )
  namesData    <- paste(names(distn) , 
    substring(paste(distn), 5), sep="")
  while(any(xx <- duplicated(namesData))) # make names unique
    namesData[xx] <- paste(namesData[xx], seq(length = sum(xx)), 
      sep = ".")
  names(data)  <- namesData
  # the ordering has changed due to 'do.call'
  data$dependency  <- factor( rep(round(dependency, rndDep) , 
    each = sizeSample)  ) 
  ans  <- list( call = match.call(), dependency = dependency, 
    sizeSample = sizeSample, distn = distn, data = data )
  class(ans)  <- "copula"
  ans
}

### EXAMPLES

rcopula () # bivariate normal with dependency 2

# bivariate normal with various (strictly positive) dependencies 
rcopula (dist = rep("norm", 2), depe = c(1,2,3) ) 

# bivariate with normal and gamma marginals
rcopula (dep = c(0.1, 2) , 
  distn = list("norm" , gamma = list(shap = 1) ) )

# Bivariate Normal plot conditioned on the dependency parameter
# Uses the first two marginals only
# arbitrary seq of positive dependency values
dep.seq  <- exp(seq(0.01, 3 , length = 12) )  - 1 
distn <- rep("norm", 2) # or use 'list("norm", norm = list() )' etc
data.nd  <- rcopula (dep = dep.seq, sizeSample = 1000, 
  di = distn )$data
xyplot(formula = data.nd[[2]] ~ data.nd[[1]] | dependency ,  
  panel = function(x, y, subscripts, groups, ...) 
  {  panel.grid(h= -1, v = -1 , lwd =.2 , lty=7, col=1) 
    panel.xyplot(x , y , col = 6, lty = 1, ...)  
  } ,
  strip = function(...) 
   strip.default ( ... , strip.names =c(F,F) , style = 1 ),
  data = data.nd, 
  as.table = T, type="p", scales = list(alternating = F),
  main = list(paste("Bivariate normal with changing dependency",
    sep="") ) , 
  sub = list(paste("Marginals are N(0,1)",  sep="") ) , 
  xlab = names(data.nd)[1] , ylab = names(data.nd)[2] 
)

# Trivariate plot conditioned on the dependency parameter
# arbitrary seq of positive dependency values
dep.seq  <- exp(seq(0.01, 3 , length = 12) )  - 1 
# marginals are (arbitrarily) weibull, cauchy, t & beta
distn <- list(weibull = list(shap = 2) , "cauchy" , 
  t = list(df = 3), beta = list(shape1 = 1, shape2 = 1) )
data.nd  <- rcopula (dep = dep.seq, sizeSample = 1000, 
  di = distn , rndDep = 2 )$data
# looks at first 3 marginals only
cloud(data.nd[[3]] ~ data.nd[[1]] * data.nd[[2]] | dependency ,
  data = data.nd, as.table = T, scales = list(alternating = F),
  subset = as.logical(match(dependency , 
    levels(dependency)[ c(1, 1:3*4) ] , nomatch = 0) ) , 
  distance = .05, screen = list(z = 120, x = -60, y = 0), 
  col = 6, cex = 3,
  strip = function(...) 
   strip.default ( ... , strip.names =c(T,T) , style = 1 ),
  main = list(paste("Trivariate normal with changing depndncy", 
    sep="") ) , 
  sub = list(paste("Marginals are N(0,1)",  sep="") ) , 
  xlab = names(data.nd)[1] , ylab = names(data.nd)[2], 
  zlab = names(data.nd)[3]
)

# visually check that histograms of the 
# marginals are as specified
brush(data.nd, hist = T) 

# tidy up
remove( c("dep.seq", "distn", "data.nd", "rcopula"))

### END of rcopula

messages.subject: Re: [S] fortran in Splus 5.1 (summary)
messages.body_plain:
Recall that I was having trouble loading my fortran code into Splus 5.1.

It turns out that all I needed to do was modify the LOCAL_LIBS line in
my makefile to include the necessary fortran libraries.  This line
appears in the makefile that Splus generates but is commented out.
When I put it back in everything worked fine.

The line in question reads

LOCAL_LIBS="-lM77 -lF77 -lsunmath_mt"

Thanks to Nicole DePriest, Farul Ghazali, Bill Dunlap, Brian Ripley and
Henrik Aalborg Nielsen.

messages.subject: [S] summary of string
messages.body_plain:
First, thank all those who responded to my question about handling string
after a set of data. There are ways of reading it and here are the methods I
gathered.

1. Clean in word processor. The reason I didn't clean it in a word processor
is because reading the file is only a part of a simulation study. The
simulation requires 100 replicates. To save time and reduce mistakes,
automation the process is necessary.

2. Use read.table when data format is fixed and line up nicely. Such as
x1  x2  x3
x4  x5  x6
end.
missing....

3. Define ASCII format and treat every variable as string when data is not
line up nicely. Such as
  x1  x2  x4
x5
x6 x7 x8
x9
end.
Missing....

4. Use Unix. Which I don't have, so I didn't try. However, in the past,
people gave me valuable info about getting pieces .exe programs from unix or
using dos to handle data. There are really handy.

Kwang-lee

messages.subject: [S] AD Model Builder + mles
messages.body_plain:
This is not a strictly S-news posting, but may be of interest
to those who use nlmin() or nlminb() to solve optimization problems.
The program discussed below, AD Model Builder, can, however, be 
used to create DLL's that S-Plus can call.

 I wanted to report success with an optimization problem, finding
74 maximum likelihood estimates for a nonlinear model, using 
AD Model Builder (Otter Research, http://otter-rsch.com), which 
uses automatic differentiation.  My initial attempt to find 
the mle's was with nlmin() and when that failed, the next attempt 
was using NPSOL (Gill, Murray, Saunders, and Wright), which also
didn't work.

 I am definitely not an expert on optimization, so failure to 
get Splus nlmin() and NPSOL to work could be my own ignorance!

 With that caveat in mind, Dave Fournier (Otter Research)
used AD Model Builder to create an executeable program which
calculated the 74 estimates in less than a minute on a Pentium 
300 class PC.  And it output the variance-covariance matrix
for the mles.  Using Splus' nlmin(), it took typically 20 minutes 
to reach ~150 iterations at which point it usually hung, or 
occasionally came back with a false convergence message.  Using 
NPSOL, a Fortran program, results would come back within about 
3 or 4 minutes, reporting failure to converge, numerical 
conditioning problems.  For both nlmin() and NPSOL I tried lots 
of different starting values, initial step sizes, etc but always 
failed to get the mles.  Again I'm sure there are better ways to 
set up the objective function and run nlmin() or NPSOL, and these 
may solve the convergence problems. With AD Model Builder even 
relatively "naive" starting values did not yield convergence 
problems, however.

  Compared to the "default" approach this was not an 
overparametrized problem.  The "default" approach is a "saturated" 
model with 115 parameters (and n=115).  The data consist of 
recoveries of tagged juvenile chinook salmon released at two 
locations, upstream and downstream.  The recoveries of upstream 
releases occur at the downstream release location and in the 
ocean, while the recoveries of the downstream releases occur 
only in the ocean.  

 The "standard" approach for analyzing these 3 recovery types for 
a given pair of releases is to assume a trinomial model for the 2 
recovery categories of upstream releases and a binomial model for 
the 1 recovery category of downstream releases.   For a given pair 
of releases, 3 parameters are estimated: survival to downstream 
point (S), capture rate at the downstream point (pd), and recovery 
rate in the ocean (po).  These parameters are easily estimated 
for a given pair of releases using maximum likelihood. 

 The problem that AD Model Builder solved was to find mle's
for a reparametrized version of the trinomial-binomial model
where survival, S, was modeled as a logit function of 7 
covariates.  There were 48 upstream releases each paired with 
one of 19 downstream releases.  The dimension of the parameter 
space was reduced from 115 to 74 but the estimation problem was 
much harder because the likelihood could no longer be partitioned
by release "pair".

  While my experience with AD Model Builder is limited to
one problem, another plus of the program is its relatively simple 
command structure.  S-Plus-like vectorization can be used, so 
it was easy for Dave Fournier to compactly write the log 
likelihood function.

Ken Newman
Division of Statistics
University of Idaho

messages.body_plain:
Here is a solution to how to fit my question (see below) about fitting a
linear mixed model.

The main problem was that the version of lme I had available was not
general enough.
By installing the last version of the package nlme (which includes an
update of lme),
fitting the model became easy. The last version (which already is
available in Splus 2000)
can be obtained from http://nlme.stat.wisc.edu/. Links to documentation
about the package
is also available from there.

Using this package, I was able to fit the model by
> fit.a <- 
> lme(fixed=logincome~AGE,random=list(FAM.NR=~1,IND.NR=~1),data=Sib1,corr=corAR1(),method="ML")
where now AGE corresponds to the explanatory variable, FAM.NR to the
highest level of grouping
(corresponding to index i below) and IND.NR to the second level of
groupig( index j below).

An alternative, using the groupedData function, is:
> SibG <- groupedData(logincome~1|FAM.NR/IND.NR,data=Sib1,outer=~AGE)
> fit.a <- 
> lme(fixed=logincome~AGE,random=~1,data=SibG,corr=corAR1(),method="ML")

Thanks to all suggestions I have recieved.

Geir

messages.subject: [S] Doubly-censored data cont.
messages.body_plain:
Dear S-news users

Hi again.  My previous message re: existing functions for the 
analysis of doubly-censored data has met with some misunderstanding -
for which I assume full responsibility.  It has also met with much
interest - so I'm hopeful that we can get some further input and
insight from other knowledgeable people out there.  Once (and if) that
happens - I will obviously post a reply detailing the findings to this
newsgroup.

Some people confused doubly-censored data with interval-censored
data and thus suggested the functions 'censor','icfit' and 
'kaplanmeier.fit'.  The reason for this confusion: the term 
"doubly censored" has been used in 2 different ways in the
literature:

1)  as described in De Gruttola & Lagakos (see below)
2)  as described in for example by Gehan (1965, Biometrika, 650-653),
    "A Generalized two-sample Wilcoxon test for doubly censored data" 
    to mean data with both left censored observations and with right
    censored observations. The icfit function in statlib by Mike Fay
    handles this type of data as well as interval censored data, but
    not the data structure I describe below. 

The situation we are interested in is as follows.  We wish to estimate
the distribution function of the length of an interval of
chronological time between two events of interest.  Let I denote the
initiating event (say, infection) and J the time of occurrence of a
subsequent event (say development of a disease).  The random variable
of interest is the interval length T = J - I.

Statistical estimation here is complicated by the fact that neither I
and J are observed exactly.  For each subject, we have the observables
(I_L,I_R,J_L,J_R).  J may be known exactly for patients who developed
the disease(J_L = J_R) or J might be right-censored if the patient has
not yet developed the disease when the observation period terminated
(J_R = inf). I and J may also both be interval censored 
(I_L <= i <= I_R), (J_L <= j <= J_R).  Presently, I am dealing with an
interval-censored I and an often right-censored J. Consequently, the
variable T is not observed exactly.

De Gruttola and Lagakos (1989) termed such data 'doubly-censored' and
generalised Turnbull's (1976) self-consistency method for
'singly-censored' data to provide a non-parametric method for the
analysis of such doubly-censored data.  Their formulation is to be
found in Biometrics 1989 45: 1-11. Later research (mostly adapted
around HIV/AIDS work) has expanded on their methodology, and we now
have methods for incorporating covariates etc (see Jewell 1994, Stats
in Medicine 13:2081-2095,Kim et al. 1993, Biometrics 49: 13-22, Sun
1995, Biometrics 51: 1096-1104).

My original question then:  Is anyone aware of an existing function in
S-PLUS that will deal adequately with this type of 'doubly-censored'
data as described above?

Thanks
Daniel
====================================================
Daniel Polakow
Department of Statistical Sciences
University of Cape Town, Rondebosch 7701
Cape Town South Africa
mobile 083-480-5338
tel 021-650-2501
fax 021-689-7578
email POLAKOW at maths.uct.ac.za

messages.subject: [S] least square means
messages.body_plain:
Some time ago it has been asked how to calculate least square means
(unfortenately I have not stored the email adress).
 
Usually they are defined as "intercept + corresponding coefficient" if the
contr.sum option is used, if only factors are involved
in the model. They are calculated this way by the following function:

lsmeans0_function(model=~.,data)
{#calculates lsmeans for the factor inccluded at the first position after ~
 #continuous covariates must be centered by subtracting their means
dname_deparse(substitute(data))
ctropt_unlist(options("contrasts"))
options(contrasts=c("contr.sum","contr.sum"))
aa_lm(model,data)
fname_attributes(terms(model))$term.labels[1]
nlevel_length(levels(data[,fname]))
acoef_aa$coefficients[1:nlevel]
bb_summary(aa)
acov_bb$cov.unscaled[1:nlevel,1:nlevel]*bb$sigma*bb$sigma
am_cbind(rep(1,nlevel),contr.sum(nlevel))
lsm_am%*%acoef
lsmcov_am%*%acov%*%t(am)
options(contrasts=ctropt)
return(data=dname,model=model,factor=fname,LSmeans=lsm,LSmeanscov=lsmcov)
}
Example: lsmeans(y~treat+A, data), where y denotes the response variable,
treat the tratment factor, A another factor,
 and data the data.frame.
The first term at the right hand side of the formula must be the factor for
which we calculate the lsmeans
(to make the function small, whithout loss of generality)

The matrix used to calculate the lsmeans from the coefficients can easily be
derived from the contr.sum matrix by
 am_cbind(rep(1,nlevel),contr.sum(nlevel)) (a small trick!)

The function computes also the covariance matrix of the lsmeans from the
covariances of coefficients 
as delivered by the summary of an lm.object. This allows to compute tests of
contrasts or confidence
limits for linear combinations of the lsmeans.

If also a numerical covariate x appears in the model, then we get different
lsmeans for different fixed
values x0 of x. Usually the overall mean is fixed (x0=xbar=overall mean of
x), The function lsmeans0 calculates
the lsmeans for x0=0. To get the lsmeans for the  xbar you must subtract
xbar from x before applying lsmeans0.
Example: lsmeans(y~treat+A+I(x-mean(x)), data) 

I hope, this answers the question.

Prof. Juergen Bock
F.Hoffmann-La Roche AG
Basel, Switzerland
email : juergen.bock at roche.com

messages.subject: SUMMARY of RE: [S] Mixed Effects model clarification
messages.subject_clean: SUMMARY of RE: [S] Mixed Effects model clarification
messages.body_plain:
Dear S+ users,

Sorry to take so long in summarizing the responses to my question (I'm still
trying to get a handle on all of it).  First, a public thank you for
everyone who helped on this:

Alan Zaslavsky
Douglas Bates
Renaud Lancelot
Joseph Lucke
Frank Lawrence
Sama LowChoy
Pat Sullivan
Anne York

Rather than posting all the e-mails that have been flying back and forth on
this, I'll try and summarize (which means if I make a mistake on something,
it's most likely my fault in trying to get a handle on all this).  First
thing to note...never actually use "_" in a label.  I was just doing that
here because I think they're easier to read than using ".".  However, if you
use a "_" as a label in Splus, bad things will happen.  My original question
is posted below.

If I am trying only to estimate the success rates in the units that are
contained in my dataset and am not concerned with serial correlation, I
could just use a glm() and treat Unit as a 20-level factor:

glm(Success~Unit + Road_Density + Season_Length, family = binomial(link =
logit),..... )

If I am trying to estimate an equation for the success rates for units in my
data set *and* outside my dataset, then I'd would use a mixed-effects model:

lme(fixed = Success ~ Road_Density + Season_Length, random = Season_Length |
Unit, data = my_data_file)

A number of people pointed out that Road_Density can not have a random
effect because there is no variability within the Units (I'm kicking myself
for having forgotten that).  The above equation will produce a mean success
rate for all units, one parameter that incorporates the effect of
Road_Density, one parameter the incorporates the effect of Season_Length,
and 40 Best Linear Unbiased Predictors (BLUPs)(one intercept predictor for
each of my 20 units and one slope predictor relating to Season_Length for
each of my 20 units).  If I want to predict success rates in a unit that was
not in my dataset, I use the mean and two parameters.  If I want to predict
success rates for a unit that was in my data set, I use the mean, the two
parameters, and that unit's BLUPs.

However, mixed-effects models do not necessarily take into account all the
residual serial correlation.  Therefore, I should also look at adding the
"corr = corAR1()" to my lme() statement to test for more complicated
correlation structure.  

The way one responder put it... I'm caught between a fixed-effects GLM to
handle my non-Gaussain Success variable, and a Gaussian random effects model
with a transformed success rate.  One solution to this is to use generalized
mixed-effects models in SAS (supposedly a GLIMMIX macro) or a program such
as MLwiN (www.ioe.ac.uk/mlwin).  I was also given the reference:"Comparisons
of Software Packages for Generalized Linear Multilevel Models" by X Zhou, AJ
Perkins, and SL Hui in The American Statistician, August 1999, 53(3),
282-290. Another solution, if I still want to go with S+, is to use
Generalized Estimating Equations (GEEs).  There are 2 S+ GEE libraries: gee
and yags (by the same author), available at
biosun1.harvard.edu/~carey/index.ssoft.html.  

Thanks for everyone's help on this!!!  If anyone else has any comments (or
corrections to what I've stated here), please feel free to contact me.  

Thanks again!

-- Andy

***********************************************************
Andy Cooper
Fisheries Conservation Biologist
National Audubon Society, Living Oceans Program
550 South Bay Ave.
Islip, New York 11751
(631) 859-1588
FAX: (631) 581-5268
acooper at audubon.org

> -----Original Message-----
> From: COOPER, Andy 
> Sent: Thursday, January 06, 2000 3:27 PM
> To: S-News
> Subject: [S] Mixed Effects model clarification
> 
> 
> 
> 
> Dear S+ users,
> 
> Please forgive me if this seems like a very basic question, 
> but this is my
> first look at mixed-effect models.  I've searched all my 
> limited resources
> (S+ manuals, Venables and Ripley (1999), and the StatLib 
> archives), and
> can't quite find the answer to my question.  I'm using S-plus 
> 2000 Release 2
> on a PC running Windows95.  Basically, I'm trying to figure 
> out if S+ is
> doing what I think/hope it's doing, and that it's actually 
> the correct thing
> to do.
> 
> I'm trying to estimate an equation to predict the success rate of elk
> hunters in Idaho.  The state is broken up into about 20 
> units, and I have
> data for each of these units for 6 years.  My dependent 
> variable is the
> success rate of hunters in each of the units in each year.  
> Some of the
> independent variables that may be related to the success rate 
> change across
> the years and differ between units (e.g. length of the 
> hunting season that
> year, what weapons were allowed that year, an estimate of the 
> elk population
> size that year, etc).  There are other independent variables 
> that describe
> the physical features of each unit that do not change over 
> time (at least at
> the scale which I'm able to measure them), such as road 
> density, percent
> area that is forested, etc. As such, my data looks a bit like 
> this (but with
> more years, more units, and more variables...these are 
> made-up numbers):
> 
> Unit  Year    Success Season_Length   Elk_Population_Size     
> Road_Density
> 1     1990    0.2             100             1000            0.05
> 1     1991    0.15            120             1020            0.05
> 1     1992    0.18            110             900             0.05
> 2     1990    0.1             60              200             0.02
> 2     1991    0.09            60              250             0.02
> 2     1992    0.15            80              220             0.02
> 
> What I am trying to do is determine which variables should be 
> included, and
> estimate the parameters for the equations :
> 
> S(i,j) = b0 + b1(j) + b2*Season_Length(i,j) + 
> b3*Pop_Size(i,j)... (eq 1)
> b1(j) = a0(j) + a1*Road_Density(j) + 
> a2*Percent_Forested_Area(j) + .... (eq
> 2)
> 
> Where S(i,j) is the properly transformed success rate in year 
> i for unit j.
> Basically, the variable that allows each unit to have a 
> separate intercept,
> b1(j), is a function of the attributes of the unit (which do 
> not change over
> time).  
> 
> To test this, what I think I would use would be the lme() 
> equation as such:
> 
> lme(Success ~ Season_Length, random = ~1|Unit, data = my_data_file)
> 
> This particular equation would allow me to test the significance of
> Season_Length, and produce estimates for the parameters b0, 
> a0(j) and b2.
> This makes sense to me, and I think it's what I'm trying to 
> do and supposed
> to do (But I could easily be wrong).
> 
> Where I get confused is when I'm trying to test for the 
> significance of
> something like Road_Density which is a continuous-valued, 
> constant attribute
> of the Unit.  From what I've been able to decipher so far, I 
> should use the
> command:
> 
> lme(Success ~ Road_Density, random = ~Road_Density|Unit, data =
> my_data_file)
> 
> if I want to allow the parameter for Road_Density to vary by 
> Unit, and the
> command:
> 
> lme(Success ~ Road_Density, random = ~1|Unit, data = my_data_file)
> 
> to test whether the parameter is the same for all Units. What 
> I can't quite
> figure out is how S+ takes into account the fact that Road_Density is
> constant over time, or whether it explicitly needs to.  For 
> instance if this
> were a repeated measures anova (using the aov() statement with
> "+Error(Unit)" included), there are separate tests for within 
> Units and
> between Units, each with the appropriate degrees of freedom.  Does the
> mixed-effect model simply take both of those into account and 
> produce an
> over-all significance test? 
> 
> Is this making any sense?  Am I interpreting all this properly?  Any
> thoughts on whether this is really what I should be doing?
> 
> Thank you for your help!!!!
> 
> Sincerely,
> Andy
> 
> ***********************************************************
> Andy Cooper
> Fisheries Conservation Biologist
> National Audubon Society, Living Oceans Program
> 550 South Bay Ave.
> Islip, New York 11751
> (631) 859-1588

messages.subject: [S] LaTeX equations in S-PLUS plots
messages.body_plain:
People on this list (and off) have asked for ways to include equations in
plots that are more complicated than can be done with the text command,
i.e. subscripts, superscripts, greek letters.  Below is a function that I
put together as one approach to this problem.

Disclaimer:  This function is NOT the MathSoft response to the problem, it
is NOT supported by MathSoft, and while I am an employee of MathSoft, this
function represents my work (play), and therefore MathSoft should not get
the blame for my mistakes. I am not one of the developers. 

All questions/comments should be sent directly to me (snow at statsci.com),
tech support is finding out about this the same way you are (and can walk
accross the hall and yell at me if you plague them to much :-).

While this is not officially supported, I will try to correct any major
blunders that get pointed out to me.  

This soulution is more of a workaround than a true solution, it actually
calls LaTeX to do the typesetting (so you have all the functionallity of
LaTeX, more than just greek letters and subscripts), then uses ImageMagick
to convert the postscript file to something that can be read in and put
into the graph by S-PLUS.  This does mean that you will need to have LaTeX
and ImageMagick installed on your computer (many Linux systems come with
them allready installed, and they are freely available for other
platforms).

A simple example of using the function:

plot(1:10, 1:10)
tmp <- latext("\\int_0^\\infty \\beta \\times x")  # click on plot 

if you want to insert the same equation/notation again (you redid the
plot), you can now do:

plot(10:1, 1:10)
latext(tmp) # click on plot to position

The equation appears in the plot on the screen and when exported or
printed (in my tests it tends to look a little better on paper than on the
screen).

There are options that allow you to: 
* specify the coordinates to insert the equation
* make the equation larger or smaller
* include a background rectangle or not
* choose which LaTeX math mode to use
* do black on white or white on black
* specify a postscript file to use instead of a LaTeX command
* pass additional information to ImageMagick to try and iprove the quality
of the included equation.

The version included below is for Unix versions, to convert it to Windows
versions: find all occurances of "unix" and replace them with "system"
(you may also want to change the default value of invert to F).

You should also set the image colors on your graphics device to shades of
grey or it may look funny.

I hope some of you find this useful,

-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
     Gregory L. Snow         |  Inertia makes the world go round,
     (Greg)                  |   Love makes the trip worth taking.
     snow at statsci.com        |
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Cut the following line and above and source into S-PLUS
===============================cut===================================

latext <- 
# This function allows you to add arbitrary LaTeX math formatting to an
# existing S-PLUS graph.
#
#  Note:  things will look best if the image colors on your graphics device
#         are set to greyscale rather than color.
#
# The arguments are:
#   text: The LaTeX string to include, i.e. "\int_0^\infty \beta x", or
#                 a matrix that has been returned from a previous call.
#   x,y:  The x and y coordinates to place the "text".
#   cex:  Character expansion, how big to make the "text", 1 means 10pt.
#   background:  Should an enclosing rectangle of the background color 
#                  (white) be plotted also.
#   inline:  If true uses LaTeX in-line mode (shorter output).
#   density:  Higher values give better quality but take more time and memory.
#   imparams:  Additional parameters to be passed to imagemagick.
#   invert:  White text on black background if T, black on white if F.
#   ps.file:  Postscript file to use instead of creating one from LaTeX.
#   ... :     Additional parameters to be passed to subplot function.
#
# You must have LaTeX and Imagemagick installed on the computer.
#
# the url for information and copies of LaTeX is:
# http://www.tug.org/
#
# The url for information and copies of imagemagick is:
# http://www.wizards.dupont.com/cristy/ImageMagick.html
#
# This function was written by Greg Snow (snow at statsci.com)
# This function is NOT supported by MathSoft and does not carry
# warrenties of any kind.  You are free to copy and use as you wish.
function(text=NULL, x = locator(1), y, cex = par("cex"), background = F, 
          inline = F, density = 1, imparams = "", invert=T, 
          ps.file = NULL, ...)
{
  if(is.matrix(text)) {
    text.mat <- text
  }
  else {
    if ( is.null(ps.file) ){
      # make LaTeX File
      sink("tempeq.tex")
      cat("\\documentclass{article}\n\\begin{document}\n")
      cat("\\thispagestyle{empty}\n\n")
      if(inline) {
          cat("$")
      }
      else {
          cat("\\[\n")
      }
      cat(text)
      if(inline) {
          cat("$")
      }
      else {
          cat("\n\\]")
      }
      cat("\n\n\\end{document}\n")
      sink()

      # convert to postscript
      unix("latex tempeq")
      unix("dvips tempeq -o")
      ps.file="tempeq.ps"
    }
    # convert to text file
    unix(paste("convert -density", round(cex * 72 * density), 
               imparams, "-crop 0x0+1+1", ps.file, "txt:tempeq.txt"))
    # read into S-PLUS
    lines <- scan("tempeq.txt", what = "", sep = "\n")
    # extract row info
    rows <- as.numeric(substring(lines, 1, regexpr(",", lines) - 1))
    # extract red component
    re.info <- regexpr(" [0-9]+", lines)
    red <- as.numeric(substring(lines, re.info + 1, re.info +
                                  attr(re.info, "match.length") - 1))
    nrows <- length(unique(rows))
    text.mat <- matrix(red, nrow = nrows)
    ncols <- dim(text.mat)[2]
    text.mat <- text.mat[, ncols:1]
  }
  text.mat2 <- text.mat
  if(!background) {
    text.mat2[text.mat2 > 240] <- NA
  }
  if( invert ){
    text.mat2 <- 255-text.mat2
  }
  size <- dim(text.mat2)/(72 * density)
  subplot(image(text.mat2, axes = F, xlab = "", ylab = "", 
                  zlim = c(0,255)), x, y, size, ...)
  invisible(text.mat)
}
