messages.subject: [S] Re: lists in function calls
messages.body_plain:
(I am replying to the list because Joe Davis' didn't include his email address 
in his original posting, and the email system here doesn't let me find out the 
original sender's address. PLEASE CAN PEOPLE EXPLICITLY INCLUDE THEIR EMAIL 
ADDRESSES WHEN POSTING TO S-NEWS!]

Joe Davis asks how to change just one or two items in a list of parameters to a 
function, while keeping the other entries at their default values. My way of 
doing this is shown in the (real) code snippets below. The code you write is 
just one line long, consisting of a call to "expand.defaults"; the supporting 
functions are admittedly a bit longer (but already exist).

hope this helps

Mark Bravington

sim.all <- function( n.sim=100, sims.to.do=1:n.sim, nt=c( 10, 20, 30), data, 
collect.stats='default', 
    postprocess=NULL, r.given.s=test.er.given.s, 
    params.for.collect.stats=list(srfamily = "GammaVE2", sm = 0.05, trace = F),
    params.for.sim=list(a = 1, b = 0.5, cv = 1, s0 = 3, Z = 0.5),
    just.data=F) {
# the list "params.for.collect.stats" (plus other things) will be passed to a 
procedure "collect.stats" using "do.call"
# the list "params.for.sim" (and other things) will be passed to a procedure 
"do.sim" using "do.call"

  expand.defaults( c( 'params.for.collect.stats', 'params.for.sim')) 

<< more code in "sim.all" >> 
# example of use of "params.for.collect.stats":
  results[ ,i]_ do.call( collect.stats, c( list( S=data$S[i,], R=data$R[i,]), 
params.for.collect.stats))
<< rest of code in "sim.all"
} # end of "sim.all"

The function "expand.defaults" changes any non-default entries in its named 
arguments. So if you call 
> sim.all( params.for.collect.stats=list( s0=27, newparam=55))
the call to "expand.defaults..." will leave "params.for.collect.stats" equal to 
list( a=1, b=0.5, cv=1, s0=27, Z=0.5, newparam=55)

expand.defaults_  function( sc, nlocal=sys.parent(), modified, default, listo) 
local({      
  default_ lapply( amatch( sys.function(), as.call( lapply( c( 'list', sc), 
as.name)))[ sc], '[[', 2)
  modified_ lapply( as.list( match.call())[ sc], eval, local=sys.parent( 2))
  for( param in names( default)[ match( names( modified), names( default), 0)]) 
{
    listo_ eval( default[[ param]])
    listo[ names( modified[[ param]])]_ modified[[ param]]
    assign( param, listo, frame=sys.nframe()) }
)}

Note that calling "expand.defaults" causes changes IN THE FRAME OF sim.all, NOT 
like usual S-PLUS behaviour. This is achieved by embedding the code of 
"expand.defaults" in a call to the function "local". This function, defined 
below, is part of my collection of Splus project management & programming 
utilities, available on http://www.cefas.co.uk/splus/splus.htlml (I think). 
Full documentation on "local" is included in the utilities bundle.

local_ function( expr) { 
  sp_ sys.parent()
  nlocal_ eval( as.name( 'nlocal'), local=sp)

# Save old exit code, clear exit code, arrange tidy-up and re-installation of  
old exit code 
# when 'local' is done
  old.on.exit_ sys.on.exit()[[ nlocal]]
  if( missing( old.on.exit))
    old.on.exit_ substitute( on.exit())
  else
    old.on.exit_ substitute( on.exit( old.on.exit), list( 
old.on.exit=old.on.exit))
  
  on.exit( { 
    eval( sys.on.exit()[[nlocal]], local=nlocal) 

   # Get rid of params & temporaries
    lapply( names( params), 
        function( x, frame) if( exists( x, frame=frame)) remove( x, 
frame=frame),
      frame=nlocal)

    # Restore things hidden by params
    for( i in names( savers))
      assign( i, savers[[ i]], frame=nlocal)

    eval( old.on.exit, local=nlocal) # so old code will execute on return to 
'nlocal'
  })

  eval( expression( on.exit())[[1]], local=nlocal)

  params_ amatch( sys.function( sp), sys.call( sp))
  params_ params[ names(params)!='nlocal']
  savers_ names( params)

  if( length( params)) {
    names( savers)_ savers
    savers_ sapply( savers, exists, frame=nlocal) 
    savers_ names( savers)[ savers]
    if( length( savers)) {
      names( savers)_ savers
      savers_ lapply( savers, get, frame=nlocal) }

#   Parameters and temporary working variables:
    for( i in names( params))
      if( mode( params[[i]])!='argument') # sometimes when S routine is called 
from C
        assign( i, params[[i]], frame=nlocal) # the obvious solution!
      else { # THE NORMAL CASE: .Arguments are handled oddly and best I can do 
is...
        if( mode( params[[i]][[1]])=='missing') {
          if( mode( params[[i]][[2]])!='missing') 
             param.val_ eval( params[[i]][[2]], local=nlocal)
          else
            param.val_ params[[i]][[1]] }
        else
          param.val_ eval( params[[i]][[1]], local=sys.parent(2)) # NOTE 
CHANGE: THIS WAS local=nlocal
        assign( i, param.val, frame=nlocal) } # else NORMAL case
    } # parameter loop

# Embed 'expr' in a spurious loop so that calls to "break" will work!
  expr_ substitute( {repeat{ assign( 'answer', expr, frame=f); break}; get( 
'answer', frame=f)}, 
      list( expr=substitute( expr), f=sys.nframe()))

# The business end!

messages.subject: [S] Spatial statistics on an irregular surface
messages.subject_clean: [S] Spatial statistics on an irregular surface
messages.body_plain:
Greetings,

Maybe off-topic, maybe not but...   We have some data which are the
distribution of points on an irregular 3-d surface (so we have (x,y,z)
values which define the points and (at least approximately) the
surface). We are interested in quantifying and testing hypotheses about
the clustering on that surface (a cell membrane) - and comparing the
distributions after various treatments.  The surface is very irregular
and maybe even a bit folded in places, which doesn't help, on the other
hand it may be possible to get more accurate surface co-ordinates in the
future.

Can anyone point me to any methods and/or software for handling such
data?  Clearly one can get a reasonable nearest-neighbour distribution,
but it is not clear how to compute a Poisson-based(actually poisson with
a minimum distance as these things are really discs) distribution with
which to compare it. How do you put random points on a complex-shaped
surface? (one thought would be to use some form of lattice which if fine
enough would approximate the surface...)

Anybody done anything like this? Any suggestions?

Cheers,

Steve.

Dr Steve Roberts
Paterson Institute for Cancer Research
Christie Hospital
Manchester M20 4BX UK
Tel: 0161 446 3074
Email: sroberts at picr.man.ac.uk

messages.subject: [S] lme and complicated repeated measures design
messages.subject_clean: [S] lme and complicated repeated measures design
messages.body_plain:
While I've quite confortable with using lme in multilevel and growth
modeling designs, I'm would appreciate a little help in a complicated (to me
anyhow) repeated measures design.

In this experiment a single subject (SUBJECT) is a member of 1 of 4
experimental groups (GROUPS).  Within each group, each subject provides data
over 10 days (DAYS).  Within each day data is collected in four sessions
(0900, 1200, 1700, and 2100) (SESSIONS).  To further complicate things each
session is composed of 10 Trials (TRIALS).  Thus, GROUP is between-subjects,
but DAYS, SESSIONS and TRIALS are within subjects.

The data has some missing values; hence my desire to estimate the model in
lme.

The researchers want to predict the subjects' score as a function of GROUPS,
DAYS, SESSIONS and TRIALS with each variable treated as a factor.  They are
interested in exploring all possible 2-way and 3-way interactions.

It makes sense to me to assume that there might be some within subject
autocorrelation for DAYS and TRIALS, but not for SESSIONS (this should
reflect a circadian rythm affect).  I can, of course, test these assumptions
with nested models.

I am clear on how to specify the fixed part of the lme model, but I'm
stymied by the random part in this particular case.  Any help would be
appreciated.

modlme<-lme(SCORE~(GROUPS+DAYS+SESSIONS+TRIALS)^3,random=?????)

Thanks,

Paul Bliese
Walter Reed Army Institute of Research
paul.bliese at na.amedd.army.mil

Paul

messages.subject: Re: [S] deriv3() question
messages.body_plain:
Ming Ji asks:

> 
> In deriv3(expr,namevec,function.arg,tag=".expr"), expr is an expression
> and is usually specified by users. Sometime, a function f(x) is too
> complicated to be written as a single expression. Can we still use
> deriv3() on f?  In my problem, f is defined by Splus coding
> f<-function(x,...){...}. 

The answer is "no".  deriv() and deriv3() are symbolic
differentiators that work with a rather limited range of
expressions usually specified by an S formula.  For it to work
with a new function "f" that you define you really need to do
quite a bit of work extending the system functions D() and
make.call().  Some of this was sketched in V&R first and second
editions (Ch 9: Non-linear regression).

Astute readers might ask "why is this so?"  In a object oriented
language why isn't it possible to devise a system whereby the
function object itself is able to carry both information on how
it is symbolically differentiated as well as how it is evaluated,
and for the symbolic differentiator to latch on to the relevant
information when it needs it?  In that way the differentiation
system could be simply extended by users adding the appropriate
differentiation information to new functions rather than by
re-coding the differentiator itself.  Isn't that the OOP payoff?

Well, don't look at me for an answer.  I have been pushing this
line for about 5 years now...

> It seems that this can be done in  ms(formula,...) because here formula
> can either be an expression or a function name. But the mode of expr in
> deriv3() is "expression" instead of "formula".

ms() does not use symbolic differentiation.  It uses numeric
differentiation, for which the function values alone are enough.

Bill Venables.

--

messages.body_plain:
(Apologies as usual for cross-posting.)

                             UNIVERSITY OF BATH

                    DEPARTMENT OF MATHEMATICAL SCIENCES

                              STATISTICS GROUP

               LECTURER/SENIOR LECTURER/READER IN STATISTICS

                  Closing date: Friday 18th February 2000

Applications are invited for a post at the Lecturer, Senior Lecturer, or
Reader level in Statistics, tenable from 1st September 2000 (or another
date by mutual agreement).  

The successful applicant will be expected to contribute to the research
and teaching activities of the group, which obtained Grade 5 in both the
1992 and 1996 Research Assessment Exercises (RAEs). 

As of 1 April 2000 the Statistics Group will comprise the following
academic staff: 

   Prof D Draper (Head of Group), Prof C Jennison (Head of Department from
   1 August 2000), Prof LCG Rogers, Prof SG Walker, Dr C Chatfield
   (Reader), Dr DG Hobson (Senior Lecturer), Mr ME Brigden, Dr SC Harris, 
   Dr MA Hurn, Dr A Robinson (Lecturers).

Members of the Statistics Group have earned a very high international
reputation for their research in the following areas:

  (i) Applied statistics, with particular emphasis on computational aspects 
        of statistical methods.
 (ii) Financial mathematics.
(iii) Probability theory.

Candidates for the advertised post should have a strong research record in
any area within statistics and probability, but an interest in one of the
above areas would be particularly welcome.

Research topics of particular interest to members of the group at the
present time include:

  Bayesian statistics (parametric and nonparametric)
  Derivative pricing and hedging          Incomplete and imperfect markets
  Interest rate modelling                 Markov chain Monte Carlo methods
  Markov processes                        Model uncertainty
  Multivariate analysis                   Optimal investment 
  Quality assessment in health/education  Sequential clinical trials
  Statistical image analysis              Stochastic differential equations
  Stochastic optimisation                 Time-series forecasting 

We have a lively group of research students and Research Officers in
statistics and probability, and frequent short and long term international
visitors. For further information about the Statistics Group see

    http://www.maths.bath.ac.uk

The Department of Mathematical Sciences is one of the largest of the
sixteen Departments making up the University of Bath. For administrative
purposes, the Department is organised into three Groups -- Mathematics,
Statistics, and Computing -- with about 50 permanent academic staff. Some
research interests cross group boundaries, and there are collaborative
research projects and joint seminars involving members of different groups.
In the 1996 RAE, the Department was awarded a Grade 5 (see note at #
below), not only in Statistics, but also in Pure Mathematics, Applied
Mathematics, and Computing (one of only three departments in the UK with
this distinction).

The Department offers BSc and MMath degree courses in a range of subjects
in the Mathematical Sciences, including (a) Statistics and (b) Mathematics
and Statistics. These degrees are based on a common first year course (with
minor exceptions) and progressive specialisation thereafter. About half the
students take the BSc course over four years, spending the third year on
placement in industry or a research establishment. This industrial training
is a highly valued part of the course and is one of the distinctive
features that helps Bath maintain one of the highest quality intakes of
students in the UK (the Departmental average A-level points in recent years
across the typical entering cohort of about 170 students has exceeded 27;
see note at # below). The Department has a computer support team of three
full-time members of staff, and an excellent network of high-speed CPU and
file servers.

Any queries about the academic aspects of the post should be directed to 
Prof David Draper (tel. 01225 826222, email d.draper at maths.bath.ac.uk), 
Prof Chris Jennison (tel. 01225 826468, email cj at maths.bath.ac.uk), or
Prof Chris Rogers (tel. 01225 826224, email lcgr at maths.bath.ac.uk).

                               APPLICATIONS

For further particulars (please quote Reference 00/21) and an application
form, please contact Peter J Hill, Director of Personnel, University of
Bath, Claverton Down, Bath, BA2 7AY. The closing date for applications is
Friday 18th February 2000. It is anticipated that short-listing will take
place on or about Friday March 10th, with interviews to occur on or about
Thursday March 30th.

An advertisement for this position will soon be posted at

    http://jobs.ac.uk

where it will also be possible to obtain the application form
electronically.

                            UNIVERSITY OF BATH

The academic structure of the University comprises three Faculties and the
School of Management. The Faculties are Humanities and Social Sciences
(Departments of Economics and International Development, Education,
European Studies and Modern Languages, Psychology and Social and Policy
Sciences), Engineering and Design (Departments of Architecture and Civil
Engineering, Chemical Engineering, Electrical and Electronic Engineering,
Materials Science and Engineering and Mechanical Engineering) and Science
(Departments of Biology and Biochemistry, Chemistry, Mathematical Sciences,
Pharmacy and Pharmacology, Physics and Postgraduate Medicine). Several
departments of study have developed their own self-financing centres for
research and short courses. The University has an enviable reputation for
the standard of its intake, its graduate employment record, its research
and its location on the edge of a World Heritage city (as designated by the
United Nations). Overall the University ranked 6th in the UK in the 1996
RAE.

The University of Bath, which can trace its history from the Bristol
Merchant Venturers Technical College dating back to 1894, was founded by
Royal Charter in 1966. The University has some 8,200 students who read for
degrees in Science, Technology, Arts, and Social Sciences, and has
established itself as one of the most highly-rated universities in the UK.
It attracts very highly qualified students and emphasises the relevance of
its courses to the needs of potential employers. Two-thirds of its
undergraduate students are on courses in which one of the years is spent on
external placement. The University's record of excellence in teaching,
research and sound internal management has been rewarded in the continuing
support it has received from funding bodies, industry and commerce, and
this record has earned it recognition as one of the UK's leading
institutions of higher education. In addition to its national and
international roles, the University has a growing regional importance as
the chosen partner for the development of higher education in Swindon and
Wiltshire.

The University employs about 2,000 staff and has an annual turnover of 75
million pounds. Considerable use is made of computerised systems covering
many administrative procedures, including financial reporting and budgetary
control, student records, and the planning and resourcing processes. The
University, along with other universities in the UK, is moving towards a
common management and administrative computing system for operational and
management information needs.

The University is based on a fine downland site of about 200 acres at
Claverton Down, less than two miles south-east of the city centre. The
University has been developed on a green-field site over the last
twenty-five years, so that all the buildings are relatively new and have
been designed to modern standards. Physical working conditions are
pleasant, with many buildings commanding attractive views. The facilities
on campus include a grocery shop, news agent, post office, book shop,
sub-branches of four banks, a medical centre, and a dental practice. Those
with sporting and other social interests will find a variety of clubs and
societies open to them. There are extensive catering facilities available.

In addition to those buildings used for teaching and for administration,
there are residential buildings on campus in which approximately 1,700
students reside. The city of Bath is recognised as being architecturally
one of the finest in Europe and is a very pleasant place in which to live. 
The communications network is good. Trains run at least every hour to
London 21 hours a day, with the fastest journey time about 75 minutes. The
M4 motorway runs 10 miles north of Bath and provides a convenient road
network to London, the Midlands, Wales and South West England.

Westwood Nursery, which is on site at Claverton Down, offers competitively
priced nursery care for children from two years of age until they start
school. The nursery is open throughout the year and, subject to the
availability of places, children may attend on a full or part time basis.

Appointments are offered subject to the University receiving a satisfactory
health report from the University Medical Officer. This is normally
undertaken on the basis of a review of a confidential medical
questionnaire. Smoking of any kind is prohibited in all University
buildings, with the exception of some bar and residential areas.

messages.subject: [S] KDD-2000 Call for Tutorial Proposals
messages.body_plain:
KDD-2000 Call for Tutorial Proposals
                      
                           KDD-2000:
           The Sixth ACM SIGKDD International Conference
             on Knowledge Discovery and Data Mining

               August 20-23, 2000, Boston, MA, USA

                 http://www.acm.org/sigkdd/kdd2000

                      Call for Proposals
   http://www.acm.org/sigs/sigkdd/kdd2000/KDD2000-TutorialsCFP.htm

              Tutorial Proposals due:  March 6, 2000

KDD-2000 Tutorials Chair:  Raymond Ng, University of British
                           Columbia, (rng at cs.ubc.ca)

Tutorials have become an essential component in many conferences and
workshops related to data mining. This is partly because data mining is
highly inter-disciplinary in nature. But this is also because
tremendous progress in research and development has been made in the
past decade.  As a tradition, KDD conferences have been offering high
quality tutorials on the very many aspects of data mining. 

For KDD-2000, we are seeking proposals for 4 to 8 tutorials. An ideal
tutorial should stimulate synergy among the three different
sub-communities in data mining, i.e., databases, machine learning and
statistics. It may discuss novel data mining techniques, successful
applications in data mining, and/or theme-oriented comprehensive
surveys.

Submission Details:
Deadline: March 6, 2000
Soft Copy to: rng at cs.ubc.ca (postscript preferred), or
Hard Copy to: Raymond Ng, 2366 Main Mall, UBC, Vancouver, B.C. Canada V6T
1Z4

Proposal Details:
1) Apart from the title of the proposal, it must clearly identify
   the intended audience, e.g., novice learners on statistical
   techniques, expert researchers on classification. An ideal tutorial
   should have an intended audience broader than a single sub-community.

2) The proposal must identify the amount of time intended. For KDD-2000,
   tutorials may be 2-hour, 3-hour or 4-hour long. 

3) Enough materials should be included in the proposal to provide a sense
   of both the scope and depth of the tutorial. (In fact, the more
   detailed, the better.) In the proposal, it may specify the material to be

   covered for a 2-hour, 3-hour and/or 4-hour period.

4) The proposal should include a short biography of each tutor (including
Web 
   address). For the proposed subject matter, on the one hand, the
   tutor must have appropriate qualification. On the other hand, the
   tutor must NOT focus mainly on his/her research results. KDD
   tutorials are not the forum for promoting one's research or product.
   If for certain parts of the tutorial, the material comes directly
   from the tutor's own research or product, please indicate that in the
   proposal.
   
For further information, please contact Raymond Ng (rng at cs.ubc.ca).

messages.subject: [S] RE: Batch Jobs in Windows 98
messages.body_plain:
You can run scheduled jobs using the Windows Task Scheduler.

Programs | Accessories | System Tools | Scheduled Tasks

Use the Settings and Schedule tab to control the execution. It is a little
tricky to run programs sequentially. I suggest you either estimate the run
time conservatively between jobs, or try specifying the computer idle for a
number of minutes before starting the next job (though the computer may
never be idle if on a network with email and virus checking).

I have used Windows 98 like this and it works OK once you get the hang of
it.

For smaller batch jobs you can use the source() command under SPlus to
execute a number of script files, though only one SPlus session is invoked.

On Mon, 17 Jan 2000 08:57:24 +1300, you wrote:

>You can run scheduled jobs using the Windows Task Scheduler.
>
>Programs | Accessories | System Tools | Scheduled Tasks
>
>Use the Settings and Schedule tab to control the execution. It is a little
>tricky to run programs sequentially.

A simple way to run programs sequentially is to use a .BAT file
together with the "start /w" command.  I don't remember the syntax to
start a batch job in SPLUS, but you write something like this to run a
sequence of them:

start /w splus job1
start /w splus job2
start /w splus job3
 ...

Put these lines in a file named something like "runjobs.bat", then run
it.

This assumes that your jobs cause SPLUS to exit at the end.  The batch
file will wait for that to happen before it starts the next one.

Duncan Murdoch

messages.subject: [S] Finding most closely matching element
messages.body_plain:
Suppose we have a vector y and z (of differing lengths) and we wish
to find, for each z,  which element of (subscript) of y is closest to each 
value of z.
The folllowing works:

apply(outer(z, y), function(a,b)abs(a-b)), 1, order)[1,]

But this can require a lot of  memory for some cases.  The following almost
works, is blazing fast, and requires minimal memory:

approx(y, 1:length(y), xout=z, rule=2, method='constant')$y

For example:

y <- c( -1.5, 1.22, 0.705, 0.0653, -0.436, -0.66)
z <- c(1.09, -0.974, -0.149, -0.253, -0.084, 1.33, 1.27, 0.368)
apply(outer(z, y, function(a,b)abs(a-b)), 1, order)[1,]
[1] 2 6 4 5 4 2 2 4   # The right answer

> approx(y, 1:length(y), xout=z, rule=2, method='constant')$y
[1] 3 1 5 5 5 2 2 4
> approx(y, 1:length(y), xout=z, rule=2, method='constant', f=1)$y
[1] 2 6 4 4 4 2 2 3

Does anyone see a very fast way to get the desired result?

Thanks  -Frank

--
Frank E Harrell Jr
Professor of Biostatistics and Statistics
Division of Biostatistics and Epidemiology
Department of Health Evaluation Sciences
University of Virginia School of Medicine
http://hesweb1.med.virginia.edu/biostat

messages.body_plain:
Frank--

(I'm replying to the list as there's no email address in your message)--

The trick is to also look at the mid-points between each pair of sorted 
y-elements. The following routine does the trick

find.nearest_ function( y, z) {
  ry_ rank( y)
  y_ sort( y)
  ly_ length( y)
  ydiff_ (y[-1]+y[-ly])/2
  yy_ c( t( matrix( c( y, ydiff, 0), ncol=2)))[ -(ly+ly)] # lazy way to get  
sorted elements of y, interspersed with mid-points
  a_ approx( yy, 1:(2*ly-1), z, method='constant', rule=2)$y / 2
  ry[ round( a+0.6)] # maps x & x.5 to (x+1) where x is an integer
}

Well to be honest I've not checked this very thoroughly. But it does reproduce 
the desired answer in the example you gave.

Hope this helps

cheers
Mark

messages.subject: Re: [S] Finding most closely matching element
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to Alan Zaslavsky <zaslavsk at hcp.med.harvard.edu> for a very fast 
solution.

Here is what Alan was so kind to send:

y.order_order(y)
y.sort_y[y.order]
y.order[round(approx(y.sort, 1:length(y), xout=z, rule=2, method='linear')$y)]

or equivalently

order(y)[round(approx(sort(y), 1:length(y), xout=z, rule=2, method='linear')$y)]

The idea is to interpolate (after arranging in order) and then round the
index, since the fractional part of the index represents the relative
distance from the two adjacent values.

Thanks Alan.  Thanks also to Mark Bravington for sending another solution.  
-Frank

messages.subject: Re: [S] Finding most closely matching element
messages.body_plain:
Frank E Harrell Jr <fharrell at virginia.edu> posed the question:
> 
> Suppose we have a vector y and z (of differing lengths) and we
> wish to find, for each z, which element of (subscript) of y is
> closest to each value of z.  [What is the quickest way to do it?]

Curiously only recently I had a two-dimensional version of
precisely this problem, which I now propose as a challenge for
anyone with a taste for such things.  As far as I can see no
variation on Alan Zaslavski's ingenious refinement of Frank's
outline fast solution will help much.  

Here is the generic problem:

--

We have a target set of 2d points prescribed by two vectors, say
Lat and Lon, and a reference 2d set prescribed by Lat0 and Lon0.

For each point in the target set find the index of the closest
point to it in the reference set, in the sense of Euclidean
distance.

--

To give some ideal of scale for the practical problem, the
reference set, (Lat0, Lon0) is a fine but discrete representation
of a section of the northern Australian coastline, about 15000
points, and the target set, (Lat, Lon), are the locations of
trawl stations at sea, about 30000 in a typical run.  The problem
is really to find the distance to dry land of each of the trawl
stations, but the index of the nearest point on the coastline is
enough for now.

I must confess I solved it by the most obvious seek-and-find
method and a couple of lines of C code, and it works quite well
enough, but I would still like to see a portable solution in
native S using at most S-PLUS built-ins.  A learned colleague
(guess!) has already pointed to knn1 in the class library, as
well as to some tricks using the Voronoi tesselation, but
essentially the problem is still open.

Bill Venables.

-- 
-----------------------------------------------------------------

messages.body_plain:
## Well, my solution is not really allowable I think due to the fact that 
## it uses a module, but here it is. It is more approriate for the
## multidimensional examples, for example the coastline thing. 
## I assume somebody might have posted this already so apologies in that
## case, I have just deleted a chunk of S-news as I have been away. 

## The only problem line!
module(spatial)

## Numbers of base and test points
N <- 15000; M <- 30000

## Coastline data (in 4-d space-time for fun)
base.pts <- matrix(rnorm(N*4), ncol=4)

## test points.
test.pts <- matrix(rnorm(M*4), ncol=4)

## Build a quad tree with the base points.
base.tree <- quad.tree(base.pts))

## filter test points down quad tree tree to find neighbours
results <- find.neighbor(test.pts, quadtree=base.tree, k=1)

## Note that this gives both of the indices and the distance...

## For this example unix.time tells me

## 0.3300004005 0.0099999905 1.0000000000 0.0000000000 0.0000000000
## 4.7899999614 0.0799999237 5.0000000000 0.0000000000 0.0000000000

## for the two pertinant calls. 

## Elapsed time is about 4-5 secs.
## Version 3.4 Release 1 for Silicon Graphics Iris, IRIX 5.3 : 1996 

## For 1e6  points in base and test sets it takes about 5 minutes. 
## This  method has obvious advantages and disadvantages, certainly in the
## univariate case this is a chainsaw and the problem might be termed
## extremely soft butter. 

##              SDB

messages.subject_clean: [S] Summary: using lists in function calls
messages.body_plain:
Dear Snews,

I was supposed to send this summary out on Friday, but I got distracted and 
didn't make it.

I am indebted to those who kindly responded to my request:
Mark Bravington, Bert Gunter,Duncan Murdoch, and Tiim Hesterberg

Basically, there were two approaches. The first approach is to
1) have a default list internal to the function,
2) have the user pass in non-default values as a list
3) loop through the user-defined list and update the default list

To implement this approach, I did the following:
1) created a list with all of the defaults outside of the function (there are a 
number of default lists that I need to maintain)
2) wrote a blindingly simple function "updateList" which does the update above
3) go through all of the default lists that need to be updated with 
user-defined values

This allows me to change the default settings very easily and also do run-time 
changes.

The second approach, sent by Mark Bravington to the list is really what I was 
looking for in that it allows me to access the named list in the function 
definition for filling out the defaults. The advantage of this is that I don't 
need the defaults definition as above. The disadvantage is that you have to 
edit the function to change the default settings. Of course, there are 
situations where you will want one or the other, so having both
methods is great.

Just for the sake of completeness, I will append Mark's message here, even 
though it was already posted to the group.

Thank you very much for your quick responses!

Best regards,
jcd
--
Joseph C. Davis, Ph.D                         PDF Solutions
101 W. Renner Rd. Ste 100      Consulting and Software for
Richardson, TX 75082            Semiconductor Manufacturing
(972) 889-3025                               fax: (972) 889-2486

"Mark Bravington FSMG CEFAS (DN=MVB00, RECIPIENTS, LOWESTOFT, CEFAS)" wrote:

> (I am replying to the list because Joe Davis' didn't include his email 
> address in his original posting, and the email system here doesn't let me 
> find out the original sender's address. PLEASE CAN PEOPLE EXPLICITLY INCLUDE 
> THEIR EMAIL ADDRESSES WHEN POSTING TO S-NEWS!]
>
> Joe Davis asks how to change just one or two items in a list of parameters to 
> a function, while keeping the other entries at their default values. My way 
> of doing this is shown in the (real) code snippets below. The code you write 
> is just one line long, consisting of a call to "expand.defaults"; the 
> supporting functions are admittedly a bit longer (but already exist).
>
> hope this helps
>
> Mark Bravington
>
> sim.all <- function( n.sim=100, sims.to.do=1:n.sim, nt=c( 10, 20, 30), data, 
> collect.stats='default',
>     postprocess=NULL, r.given.s=test.er.given.s,
>     params.for.collect.stats=list(srfamily = "GammaVE2", sm = 0.05, trace = 
> F),
>     params.for.sim=list(a = 1, b = 0.5, cv = 1, s0 = 3, Z = 0.5),
>     just.data=F) {
> # the list "params.for.collect.stats" (plus other things) will be passed to a 
> procedure "collect.stats" using "do.call"
> # the list "params.for.sim" (and other things) will be passed to a procedure 
> "do.sim" using "do.call"
>
>   expand.defaults( c( 'params.for.collect.stats', 'params.for.sim'))
>
> << more code in "sim.all" >>
> # example of use of "params.for.collect.stats":
>   results[ ,i]_ do.call( collect.stats, c( list( S=data$S[i,], R=data$R[i,]), 
> params.for.collect.stats))
> << rest of code in "sim.all"
> } # end of "sim.all"
>
> The function "expand.defaults" changes any non-default entries in its named 
> arguments. So if you call
> > sim.all( params.for.collect.stats=list( s0=27, newparam=55))
> the call to "expand.defaults..." will leave "params.for.collect.stats" equal 
> to
> list( a=1, b=0.5, cv=1, s0=27, Z=0.5, newparam=55)
>
> expand.defaults_  function( sc, nlocal=sys.parent(), modified, default, 
> listo) local({
>   default_ lapply( amatch( sys.function(), as.call( lapply( c( 'list', sc), 
> as.name)))[ sc], '[[', 2)
>   modified_ lapply( as.list( match.call())[ sc], eval, local=sys.parent( 2))
>   for( param in names( default)[ match( names( modified), names( default), 
> 0)]) {
>     listo_ eval( default[[ param]])
>     listo[ names( modified[[ param]])]_ modified[[ param]]
>     assign( param, listo, frame=sys.nframe()) }
> )}
>
> Note that calling "expand.defaults" causes changes IN THE FRAME OF sim.all, 
> NOT like usual S-PLUS behaviour. This is achieved by embedding the code of 
> "expand.defaults" in a call to the function "local". This function, defined 
> below, is part of my collection of Splus project management & programming 
> utilities, available on http://www.cefas.co.uk/splus/splus.htlml (I think). 
> Full documentation on "local" is included in the utilities bundle.
>
> local_ function( expr) {
>   sp_ sys.parent()
>   nlocal_ eval( as.name( 'nlocal'), local=sp)
>
> # Save old exit code, clear exit code, arrange tidy-up and re-installation of 
>  old exit code
> # when 'local' is done
>   old.on.exit_ sys.on.exit()[[ nlocal]]
>   if( missing( old.on.exit))
>     old.on.exit_ substitute( on.exit())
>   else
>     old.on.exit_ substitute( on.exit( old.on.exit), list( 
> old.on.exit=old.on.exit))
>
>   on.exit( {
>     eval( sys.on.exit()[[nlocal]], local=nlocal)
>
>    # Get rid of params & temporaries
>     lapply( names( params),
>         function( x, frame) if( exists( x, frame=frame)) remove( x, 
> frame=frame),
>       frame=nlocal)
>
>     # Restore things hidden by params
>     for( i in names( savers))
>       assign( i, savers[[ i]], frame=nlocal)
>
>     eval( old.on.exit, local=nlocal) # so old code will execute on return to 
> 'nlocal'
>   })
>
>   eval( expression( on.exit())[[1]], local=nlocal)
>
>   params_ amatch( sys.function( sp), sys.call( sp))
>   params_ params[ names(params)!='nlocal']
>   savers_ names( params)
>
>   if( length( params)) {
>     names( savers)_ savers
>     savers_ sapply( savers, exists, frame=nlocal)
>     savers_ names( savers)[ savers]
>     if( length( savers)) {
>       names( savers)_ savers
>       savers_ lapply( savers, get, frame=nlocal) }
>
> #   Parameters and temporary working variables:
>     for( i in names( params))
>       if( mode( params[[i]])!='argument') # sometimes when S routine is 
> called from C
>         assign( i, params[[i]], frame=nlocal) # the obvious solution!
>       else { # THE NORMAL CASE: .Arguments are handled oddly and best I can 
> do is...
>         if( mode( params[[i]][[1]])=='missing') {
>           if( mode( params[[i]][[2]])!='missing')
>              param.val_ eval( params[[i]][[2]], local=nlocal)
>           else
>             param.val_ params[[i]][[1]] }
>         else
>           param.val_ eval( params[[i]][[1]], local=sys.parent(2)) # NOTE 
> CHANGE: THIS WAS local=nlocal
>         assign( i, param.val, frame=nlocal) } # else NORMAL case
>     } # parameter loop
>
> # Embed 'expr' in a spurious loop so that calls to "break" will work!
>   expr_ substitute( {repeat{ assign( 'answer', expr, frame=f); break}; get( 
> 'answer', frame=f)},
>       list( expr=substitute( expr), f=sys.nframe()))
>
> # The business end!
>   eval( expr, nlocal)
> }
>

messages.subject: RE: [S] Finding most closely matching element
messages.body_plain:
Bill,

I don't see why you can't use Alan and Frank's method twice to get indices
for the x's and y's separately. Since it is a reference set of points, you
can easily relate the indices of the separate coordinates to the indices of
the reference grid, as below.

x0<-0:10;y0<-0:10;xyref<-data.matrix(expand.grid(x=x0,y=y0))
x<-runif(20,0,10);y<-runif(20,0,10)
plot(xyref)
points(x,y,pch=4,col=2)
iy <- order(y0)[round(approx(sort(y0), 1:length(y0), xout=y, rule=2,
method='linear')$y)]
ix <- order(x0)[round(approx(sort(x0), 1:length(x0), xout=x, rule=2,
method='linear')$y)]
ind <- matrix(1:121,11,11)[cbind(ix,iy)]
points(data.matrix(xyref)[ind,],pch=3,col=3)

Nick Ellis

-----Original Message-----
From: owner-s-news at wubios.wustl.edu
[mailto:owner-s-news at wubios.wustl.edu]On Behalf Of Bill Venables
Sent: Tuesday, 18 January 2000 0:53
To: S-news at wubios.wustl.edu
Subject: Re: [S] Finding most closely matching element

Frank E Harrell Jr <fharrell at virginia.edu> posed the question:
>
> Suppose we have a vector y and z (of differing lengths) and we
> wish to find, for each z, which element of (subscript) of y is
> closest to each value of z.  [What is the quickest way to do it?]

Curiously only recently I had a two-dimensional version of
precisely this problem, which I now propose as a challenge for
anyone with a taste for such things.  As far as I can see no
variation on Alan Zaslavski's ingenious refinement of Frank's
outline fast solution will help much.

Here is the generic problem:

--

We have a target set of 2d points prescribed by two vectors, say
Lat and Lon, and a reference 2d set prescribed by Lat0 and Lon0.

For each point in the target set find the index of the closest
point to it in the reference set, in the sense of Euclidean
distance.

--

To give some ideal of scale for the practical problem, the
reference set, (Lat0, Lon0) is a fine but discrete representation
of a section of the northern Australian coastline, about 15000
points, and the target set, (Lat, Lon), are the locations of
trawl stations at sea, about 30000 in a typical run.  The problem
is really to find the distance to dry land of each of the trawl
stations, but the index of the nearest point on the coastline is
enough for now.

I must confess I solved it by the most obvious seek-and-find
method and a couple of lines of C code, and it works quite well
enough, but I would still like to see a portable solution in
native S using at most S-PLUS built-ins.  A learned colleague
(guess!) has already pointed to knn1 in the class library, as
well as to some tricks using the Voronoi tesselation, but
essentially the problem is still open.

Bill Venables.

multicomp(test2.aov,focus="group",adjust=list(utterance=c("t","s","sh")),

messages.subject: [S] contrasts in survival analysis
messages.body_plain:
Hello S-news,

I'm doing some survival analysis on SPLUS 2000. I was quite surprised by
the following results I get using two different options of contrasts.

In my first model I've used the treatment contrasts to interpret easyly
the coefficients (V&R 2nd ed., p.200) and in the second one the default
helmert contrasts. 

The results show that p-values and Schoenfeld residuals change. So does
it means that changing the coding of factors modify the p-values and
residuals?

Can someone explain me why p-value and schoenfeld residuals are
different with these two kinds of contrasts? 

Thanks a lot for your help.

messages.subject: [S] Summing up values
messages.body_plain:
I have an array of data that has in the first two columns the indices of
another array that I want to accumulate a sum and the 3rd column is the
value: e.g.,

> a.1
     [,1] [,2] [,3]
[1,]    1    1   10
[2,]    1    1   20
[3,]    1    1   30
[4,]    2    1    1
[5,]    2    1    2
[6,]    3    1  100
>

What I want to create is an array that looks like: (only a single column
for the example)

60
4
100

But when I typed the command:

>  mat[a.1[,1:2]] _ mat[a.1[,1:2]] + a.1[,3]

I got the result:

> mat
     [,1]
[1,]   30
[2,]    2
[3,]  100

What it looks like is that I was not accumulating the values in each slot,
but the assignment (mat[a.1[,1:2]] _ mat[a.1[,1:2]] + a.1[,3])  was just
putting the 'last' value into the entry.

How can I do this without going through a loop?  The table has about
200,000 entries that will be summaried into an array of about 400 X 500
(many missing values which will be zero)

Jim Holtman
james.holtman at convergys.com

messages.subject: Re: [S] key overlapping axis
messages.body_plain:
Thanks to all who responded to my query (posted below) regarding key
placement overlapping with the right axis.  The easiest for me 
to use was the transparent=T option:

key(70,3.5,border=0,cex=.7,text=list(paste(c(0:6)," = ",
c("No missing data","1 time point missing","2 time points missing",
  "3 time points missing","4 time points missing",
  "5 time points missing","6 time points missing"))),transparent=T)

Another suggestion was to modify the tck option in pars():

oldpar<-par()
par(tck=0)
axis(4,labels=F)
par(oldpar)

One could also have used the box() command after supplying the key:

key(70,3.5,border=0,cex=.7,text=list(paste(c(0:6)," = ",
c("No missing data","1 time point missing","2 time points missing",
  "3 time points missing","4 time points missing",
  "5 time points missing","6 time points missing"))),transparent=T)

box()

Lastly, the "text.width.multiplier" argument to key can be used.  This
is useful if you also want the border included:

key(70,3.5,border=1,cex=.7,text=list(paste(c(0:6)," = ",
c("No missing data","1 time point missing","2 time points missing",
  "3 time points missing","4 time points missing",
  "5 time points missing","6 time points missing"))),
  text.width.multiplier=0.7)

According to Tim Hesterberg, "S-PLUS allows too much space for text -- 
  it assumes that every letter is the width of an "m", because it
  doesn't have access to the actual width of the letters in every
  font."  

Thanks to Megan Pedger, Tim Hesterberg, Christian Keller and
Prof. Brian D. Ripley for their suggestions.  Below is a copy of my
posting and their responses.

----------------------------------------------
#My posting

Hello,

I've been using the key function to place a legend on my plot.  When I
create a Postscript file and adjust the height and width, problems
arise.  The legend prints, but there is a huge gap to the right of the end
of my text.  As a result, when I place the legend where I want it, more
often then not, the large gap overlays part of my right axis.   I tried to
use axis(4) to overwrite the offensive gap that now exists in my right
axis but I can't get it to print without any tick marks.  I had this
problem with the legend() function too.  

All suggestions welcome.  I'll summarize to the list.

A Simple Example:

postscript("test.ps", width=8, height=5.5, horizontal=T)

plot(c(0,107), c(0.5,3.5), type="n")

key(70, 3.5, border=0, cex=.7, text=list(paste(c(0:6)," = ",c("No missing
data","1 time point missing","2 time points missing","3 time points
missing","4 time points missing","5 time points missing","6 time points
missing"))))

dev.off()

Nicole

PS  I am using Version 5.1 Release 1 for Sun SPARC, SunOS 5.5 : 1999

--------------------------------------------
#Megan Pedger's response:

Try,

plot(10:1,1:10)
oldpar<-par()
par(tck=0)
axis(4,labels=F)
par(oldpar)

--------------------------------------------
#Tim Hesterberg's response:

The problems are that:
* you specified x=70; this put the text too far to the right, and put the
  box off the page; instead you can leave x (and y) unspecified, and the
  key will be put in the upper right corner
* S-PLUS allows too much space for text -- it assumes that every letter
  is the width of an "m", because it doesn't have access to the actual
  width of the letters in every font.  You can work around this using
  the "text.width.multiplier" argument to key; I usually use
        text.width.multiplier = .7
You can see where the box surrounding the key is using 
        box=T

Alternately, try
        transparent=T
with the x you specified.

--------------------------------------------
#Prof. Brian D. Ripley's response:

Try reducing the pointsize when you scale down a plot: the default
is set for a full-sized plot.

> plot(c(0,107), c(0.5,3.5), type="n")
> 
> key(70, 3.5, border=0, cex=.7, text=list(paste(c(0:6)," = ",c("No missing
> data","1 time point missing","2 time points missing","3 time points
> missing","4 time points missing","5 time points missing","6 time points
> missing"))))

Try text.width.multiplier. For me

key(70, 3.5, border=0, cex=.7, text=list(paste(c(0:6)," = ",
c("No missing data","1 time point missing","2 time points missing",
"3 time points missing","4 time points missing",
"5 time points missing","6 time points missing"))),
text.width.multiplier=0.8)

works. (I assume that line got garbled en route and should be as above.)

--------------------------------------------
#Christian Keller's response:

There are several solutions.
Probably the most elegant one is to set the argument transparent=T
in the key function.

## Solution 1: setting transparent=T

postscript("test.ps", width=8, height=5.5, horizontal=T)
plot(c(0,107), c(0.5,3.5), type="n")
key(70, 3.5, border=0, cex=.7,
    text=list(paste(c(0:6)," = ",
      c("No missing data","1 time point missing",
        "2 time points missing","3 time points missing",
        "4 time points missing","5 time points missing",
        "6 time points missing"))),
    transparent=T)    ## <--
dev.off()

## Solution 2: using box()

postscript("test.ps", width=8, height=5.5, horizontal=T)
plot(c(0,107), c(0.5,3.5), type="n")
key(70, 3.5, border=0, cex=.7,
    text=list(paste(c(0:6)," = ",
      c("No missing data","1 time point missing",
        "2 time points missing","3 time points missing",
        "4 time points missing","5 time points missing",
        "6 time points missing"))))
box()  ## <-- 
dev.off()

## Solution 3: drawing right x-axis without ticks marks

postscript("test.ps", width=8, height=5.5, horizontal=T)
plot(c(0,107), c(0.5,3.5), type="n")
key(70, 3.5, border=0, cex=.7,
    text=list(paste(c(0:6)," = ",
      c("No missing data","1 time point missing",
        "2 time points missing","3 time points missing",
        "4 time points missing","5 time points missing",
        "6 time points missing"))))
par(tck=0)          ## <--  see help(par) for details
axis(4, labels=F)   ## <--
dev.off()

______________________________________________________________________________

messages.subject: Re: [S] error in variable models
messages.body_plain:
Gerrit,

Sorry I did not see your first posting on this topic.
Check out the suite of Splus (and SAS) functions called QVF in
http://stat.tamu.edu/qvf/qvf.html
This is being developed by Ray Carroll and his colleagues in Texas A&M.

QVF is a program to do quasilikelihood estimation with measurement error in
predictors.
Some of the methods supported are Regression Calibration, SIMEX (Simulation
Extrapolation)
and Instrumental Variables.
Details about these and other procedures are described in the book:
Measurement Error in Nonlinear Models by R.J. Carroll, D. Rupert and L.A.
Stefanski (1995),
Chapman & Hall. I highly recommend this book for anyone interested in
measurement error models.

Regards,
Devan

messages.subject: [S] shewhart control charts
messages.body_plain:
I am creating a shewhart quality control chart with proportion "p" being
charted.

I have created two universes of data u1 and u2.  u1 creates the data
from which the baseline (calibration) data is drawn and u2 provides the
data from which the new data is drawn.

 u1<-c(1,rep(0,39999))
u2<-c(1,1,rep(0,1998))

We create proportions by sampling 300 times with replacement from
universe 1 (u1) and then divide by 300 placing the proportion in vector
r.  This is done 6 times to establish the calibration set.

 for (i in 1:6){r[i]<-(sum(sample(u1,300,replace=T)))/300}

We create proportions by sampling experience from universe u2 300 times
summing this experience, and then divide by 300. The proportion is
placed in vector r2.  this is repeated five times as follows:

for (i in 1:5){r2[i]<-(sum(sample(u2,300,replace=T)))/300}

I now create the shewhart chart charting both the calibration data and
the new data, recognizing that each proportion was drawn from a sample
of 300.

shewhart(qcc(r,type="p",sizes=rep(300,6)),newdata=r2,,sizes=rep(300,5),chart.all=T)

I would like to rerun these calculations multiple times (1000x) to
simulate how the chart will behave.

For each run of the chart, I would like to extract the following
information from the chart:

1. The number of instances of positive runs (runs where the outcome is
on the positive side of the calibrated mean.  Run accepts the default of
five in a row that is within the function.

2.  the number of instances of negative runs.
3.the number of events exceeding the upper limit of control defined by
the calibration data.

4.the number of events exceeding the lower limit of control defined by
the calibration data.

I would like to put these four results in a matrix.  Each chart will
generate one row with four columns of data.

I would repeat the analysis 1000X so I would have ultimately a matrix of
1000 x 4 results.

How do I extract these values from the chart object?

Sincerely,
Eran Bellin

messages.subject: [S] Re: add a line to cox.zph
messages.subject_clean: [S] Re: add a line to cox.zph
messages.body_plain:
The question was, how to add a vertical line to a cox.zph plot
at a particular time value, given that it is plotting on a transformed
scale.  
  First, to do it reliably, one can't use the original data set for
any ancillary computations, since missing values in the right-hand
side variables might have led to fewer observations in the fit.
Use the returned results of cox.zph.  
> fit <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ ph.karno, data=lung)
> zfit <- cox.zph(fit, transform='rank')
> plot(zfit)
> xx <- as.numeric(dimnames(zfit$y)[[1]])
> abline(v=sum(xx< 300))

  The returned 'y' component of cox.zph contains the scaled
Schoenfeld residuals, but also contains the original time values as
a row label.  (There is one column per dependent variable).  The
code draws a vertical line at time 300.

  For arbitrary scales, replace the last line with
> abline(v= approx(xx, zfit$x, 300)$y)

Cc:     s-news at wubios.wustl.edu <mailto:s-news at wubios.wustl.edu> 
Subject:        Re: add a line to cox.zph

  The question was, how to add a vertical line to a cox.zph plot
at a particular time value, given that it is plotting on a transformed
scale.  
  First, to do it reliably, one can't use the original data set for
any ancillary computations, since missing values in the right-hand
side variables might have led to fewer observations in the fit.
Use the returned results of cox.zph.  
> fit <- coxph(Surv(time, status) ~ ph.karno, data=lung)
> zfit <- cox.zph(fit, transform='rank')
> plot(zfit)
> xx <- as.numeric(dimnames(zfit$y)[[1]])
> abline(v=sum(xx< 300))

  The returned 'y' component of cox.zph contains the scaled
Schoenfeld residuals, but also contains the original time values as
a row label.  (There is one column per dependent variable).  The
code draws a vertical line at time 300.

  For arbitrary scales, replace the last line with
> abline(v= approx(xx, zfit$x, 300)$y)

which makes the transformation from the original (xx) to the plotted
(zfit$x) scale.  For ranks, the shorter form works because I already
know that zfit$x = 1:length(xx).  (For the purists: the shorter
form almost works -- it doesn't interpolate as we should).

        Terry Therneau

messages.subject: [S] NUOPT and math functions
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I've been using NUOPT with S+4.5 to optimize various financial problems.

However I have run up agaist some difficulties using certain functions that
are not defined in SIMPLE, the modelling language beneath NUOPT.

In particular I am frustrated not being able to use functions like max,min
and sort on simple objects. Does anyone know of a way around this? Let me
give an example, the idea being the desire to minimize the pth percentile
return from a portfolio of financial returns. The code below maximizes the
minimum return. Suppose I want to maximize the pth percentile return, in
finance speak, maximizing the Value at Risk at p%. Ideally I'd like to be
able to measure the pth percentile return for a given set of portfolio
weights.

However I can't apply sort or quantile to a simple object. (or for that
matter min or max, although these are not mentioned on p.15 of the NUOPT
manual as being unsupported). If anyone would like to get into a dialogue
with me about using NUOPT please feel free to respond to me directly, I
don't know how many people are using NUOPT out there.

Cheers

# sample returns
rmat <- matrix(rnorm(100*2),mean=0),nrow=100,ncol=2)
minret <- function(rmat,w0=rep(1/P,P)) {
 P <- ncol(rmat)
 Samples <- Set()
 Weights <- Set()
  i <- Element(set=Weights)
 k <- Element(set=Samples)
 rus <- Parameter(rmat,index=dprod(k,i))
 W0 <- Parameter(list(1:P,w0),index=i)
 w <- Variable(index=i)
 w[i] ~ W0[i]
 lambda <- Variable()
 bounds1 <- Constraint(index=k)
 V <- Objective(type="maximize")
 V ~ lambda
 # define constraints
 Sum(w[i],i)==1
 w[i] >= 0
 bounds1[k] ~ Sum(w[i]*rus[k,i],i) >= lambda
}
sys <- System(minret,rmat)
res <- solve(sys)

messages.body_plain:

                                                        - Giuseppina Gini

++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
+++++

PRE- AND POSTDOCTORAL POSITIONS AVAILABLE

Applications are invited from young researchers with an interest in joining
a four-year (2000-2003) EU network project aimed at the development of
models to predict toxicity, starting Spring 2000.
The network consists of laboratories (see the list below) working in
toxicology, computational chemistry and computer science.
Grants are available to work in one of the seven laboratories of the Network.
Grant will be from 1650 to 4320 Euro/month, depending on qualification,
experience and location. Pre-doc positions are compatible with PhD studies.
Post-doc positions require that the candidate holds (or is near to obtain)
a PhD.

Interested candidates should send an application (including CV, summary of
research interests and preferred location) to:
Dr Emilio Benfenati
Head, Laboratory of Environmental Chemistry and Toxicology
Istituto di Ricerche Farmacologiche "Mario Negri"
Via Eritrea 62, 20157 Milano, Italy
Tel: +39-02-39014420   Fax: +39-02-39001916
e-mail: benfenati at irfmn.mnegri.it
http://www.irfmn.mnegri.it/ambsal/chem-toxi/Benfenati.htm
http://www.irfmn.mnegri.it/ambsal/chem-toxi/Default.htm

Network Title: Intelligent Modelling Algorithms for the General Evaluation
of TOXicities  (IMAGETOX)

The Co-ordinator: Istituto di Ricerche Farmacologiche "Mario Negri",
Laboratory of Environmental Chemistry and Toxicology, Milan, Italy

Contact person:
Dr Emilio Benfenati (benfenati at irfmn.mnegri.it)

The Members

- Dr. M. Cronin, Liverpool John Moores University, School of Pharmacy and
Chemistry, United Kingdom (m.t.cronin at livjm.ac.uk)

- Prof. J. Hermens, Utrecht University, Research Institute of Toxicology,
Faculty of Veterinary Sciences, The Netherlands (j.hermens at ritox.vet.uu.nl)

- Prof. G. Gini, Politecnico di Milano, Dipartimento di Elettronica e
Informazione, Milano, Italy (gini at elet.polimi.it)

- Dr. M. Vracko, National Institute of Chemistry, Ljubljana, Slovenia
(marjan.vracko at ki.si)

- Prof. G. Schüürmann, UFZ Centre for Environmental Research, Leipzig,
Germany (gs at uoe.ufz.de)

- Prof. M. Karelson, University of Tartu, Department of Chemistry, Estonia
(mati at chem.ut.ee).

Conditions for EU grants

The researcher must be 35 years old or less at the time of his appointment
(allowances are possible for special cases).

The researcher must be a holder of a doctoral degree or of a degree in an
appropriate subject in Science or Engineering.

The appointment will be for a fixed-term.

The applicant must be a national of a Member State of the European
Community or of an Associated State or have resided in the European
Community for at least five years prior to his appointment.

The applicant must choose a Centre located in a state different from his
national state and he must not have carried out his activities in that
state for more than 12 of the 24 months prior to his appointment.

Research Program

The present project aims to improve the power of models for toxicity
prediction. It will take advantage of the recent advances in computer
science (such as multivariate analysis, neural networks, expert systems,
machine learning, and simulated annealing). Candidates in Computer Science
are expected to work on Machine Learning and KDD and to develop theories
and systems. These will be applied to the validation (verifying the
robustness of reported models and new predictive ones) and development for
real world applications.
Different models will be developed for (eco)toxicology and for
environmental fate prediction. For (eco)toxicology different species will
be considered, as well as different mechanisms of toxic action. In
environmental fate, partitioning between compartments in the environment
and into biota will be studied, as well as degradation.

rudimentary question I suspect it to be, I'll summarize any responses.

> Date: Thu, 20 Jan 2000 18:04:06 +0100
> From: Stefano Calza <stecalza at tin.it>

Usually one looks at methods for anova, which does this for glm and
survreg, for example.  However, you said `(cox)' which I presume means
`Cox proportional hazards fitted by coxph', and they are not fitted by
maximum likelihood nor have a deviance.  You can compare maximized
partial likelihoods, but there is no anova.coxph that I know of.

messages.subject: [S] Summary: NA's as factor level
messages.body_plain:
A little earlier I asked a question about NA's and factor levels.  Thanks to Ian
Jonsen, S.D.Byers, Peter Alspach and Bill Dunlap for such a quick reply.  The
method I thought the most elegant, my humble opinion, came from Bill Dunlap. the
solution was just to add an extra argument to the factor function, namely:
exclude = NULL.  Following you will find the original posting and Bill's
solution and comments.

Thanks to all again,

Gérald

---------------

On Thu, 20 Jan 2000, [iso-8859-1] "G?rald Jean" wrote:

> I have a column of a large data.frame which should be a factor with three
> levels.  By mistake when I defined the factor I forgot a level and as a result
> the factor variable has only two levels.  If I use na.include(variable name)
> then I have three levels again one of them being "NA".  How do I transform
this
> "NA" level to what it was supposed to be in the first place?  Any attempt I
made
> so far resulted in errors.  For exemple:
>
> > levels(ttt.2)
> [1] " A = Protege     " " B = Semi-protege" "NA"
>
> > ttt.3_factor(ttt.2, levels = levels(ttt.2), labels = c('A', 'B', 'C'))
>
> Error in factor(ttt.2, levels = levels(ttt.2), labe..: invalid labels
argument,
> len
> gth 3 should be 2 or 1

You should use exclude=NULL in the call to factor(), along with the
other arguments.  I consider this is a bug in factor().  I think that
if you give the levels explicitly (and do not give exclude explicitly)
that it should not remove any of the levels because they are on the
exclude list.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------

messages.subject: Re: [S] comparison of glims in Splus and SAS
messages.subject_clean: [S] comparison of glims in Splus and SAS
messages.body_plain:
Dear Mr. Craig,

> I am using Splus 2000 and v.6.12 of SAS both in Windows.
>
> I am attempting to fit the generalized linear model below to data from a
> fisheries trawl survey in which the number of fish caught are categorized
> into day and night.  The method is outlined in Casey and Myers. 1998.
> Canadian Journal of Fisheries and Aquatic Sciences. 55:2329-2340.
>
> I am obtaining very different parameter estimates and standard errors
> in S+ and SAS.  Has anyone compared the output of glims between SAS and
> S+ or have insight as to why the results differ between the programs?
> I've verifed that the data are being input correctly, but am a relatively
> new user to both of these programs.  Will sum unless this is a no-brainer!
>
> S+ call:
> glm(formula=catchday/catchtotal~(-1)+daytime+offset(setoff),
> family=binomial,link=logit)
>
> SAS code:
> proc genmod; class daytime;
>         model catchday/catchtotal=daytime /link=logit dist=binomial
> offset=setoff noint;

from my point of view, there exist some points which may be result in different
output from SAS and S-PLUS.
The following list is not complete.

(a) SAS and S-PLUS often treat discrete explanatory variables in a different 
manner.
     In SAS the reference category is often the "last" category depending of the
     ORDER=... statement.
     In S-PLUS one can define how discrete explanatory variables are coded, 
e.g. check
     options (contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.treatment"))
     In S-PLUS this may be the "first" category.
(b) In SAS one can specify in the MODEL-Statement, whether
      TYPE-I or TYPE-III tests are computed and whether these tests
      are WALD tests or Likelihood Ratio tests.
      What kind of tests did you specify in SAS or S-PLUS?
(c) If you fit a logistic regression model it can happen that different programs
     may fit the number of (y_i=1) or the number of (y_i=0), e.g.
     PROC LOGISTIC, PROC CATMOD or PROC GENMOD in SAS.
    Often there is an option to specify this (DESCENDING in PROC LOGISTIC).
    (From my point of view this is perhaps no problem in your program.)
(d) In logistic regression models the classical estimator is the maximum
     likelihood estimator. However, it is well-known there the ML-estimates
     do NOT exist, if there is complete separation or quasi-complete separation,
     c.f. Albert and Anderson(1984) or Santner and Duffy (1986,Biometrika).
     The ML-estimates are computed in an iterative manner, but it can happen, 
that
    the algorithm does not converge. In SAS PROC GENMOD there is an
    option to get the whole iteration history (ITPRINT).
    Do you have convergence for your data set?
   Does SAS output a warning, that there might be complete separation or 
quasi-complete separation
   in your data set?
(e) Please check whether the offset term is treated equal in both programs.

Good luck,
Andreas

messages.subject: [S] predict.discrim() problem
messages.body_plain:
Hello all:

I've recently begun using the SPlus 2000 discrim() function again.  I'm 
interested in performing 10-fold cross validation on the data and I've 
adapted the generic cross-validation functions described in Venables & 
Ripley (2nd edition, p.493, 3rd edition, p.361).  Anyway, the functions are 
below.

To make a long story short, the functions below work perfectly with when 
the VR3 MASS library functions lda(), multinom(), and qda(), are 
substituted, but fail with discrim().  It looks like the cross validation 
fails in predict.discrim(), not in discrim() itself.  I've gone through the 
predict.discrim code and can't figure out what it variable it thinks is 
supposed to be there that isn't there.  There is a comment in the 
predict.discrim() code about forcing factors when there are 0 cases in a 
group.  This is certainly possible with the sampling protocol, but lda() 
and qda() don't seem to be fazed by it.  Since predict.discrim is modelled 
after predict.lda, I can't quite figure what is going wrong.

What (no doubt, painfully obvious) thing am I missing here?

I'm reasonably certain that the problem lies either with predict.discrim or 
the call I've written to it.  The generic cross validation code in VR works 
too well with other routines for me to think that there is a problem with 
that part.  I've written to Brian Ripley, thinking the problem might have 
been there, but after playing with it some more, I do not think that is the 
issue.

Any help or suggestions appreciated.

Full code and error message below.  Sorry for the (lack of) 
formatting.  Hard to paste from the SPlus 2000 script editor into an email 
client, strip the HTML formatting and retain the correct spacing/indenting.

Code:

========================================
rand <-sample(10, 237, replace=T)
mydata<-hominoid[,c(3,6:15)]
con<-function(x,y)
{
        tab<-table(x,y)
        print(tab)
        diag(tab)<-0
        cat("error rate = ", round(100*sum(tab)/length(x),2), "%\n")
        invisible()
}

CVtest <-function(fitfn, predfn, ...)
{
        res <- mydata$genus
        for(i in sort(unique(rand))) {
                cat("fold", i, "\n", sep = "")
                learn <- fitfn(rand != i, ...)
                res[rand == i] <- predfn(learn, rand == i)
                NULL
        }
        res
}

res.discrim<-CVtest(

	function(x, ...) discrim(genus~., data=mydata[x,], 
family=Canonical("linear"), prior="uniform"),

	function(obj, x) predict(obj, mydata[x,])$groups)

==============================================

OUTPUT:

discrim(genus ~ ., data = mydata[x,  ], family =
        Canonical("linear"), prior = "uniform"),
        function(obj, x)
predict(obj, mydata[x,  ])$groups)
fold1
Error in predict.discrim(obj, mydata..: newdata is missing variable(s) .

I have also had problems of this kind going from S-PLUS 5.1
release 2 on Sun SPARC solaris 7 to S-PLUS 2000.  I believe the
problem lies with data.dump on S-PLUS 5.1 which seems to be
seriously broken, especially in the way it handles large data
sets.  Components of data frames seems to drop out, so that you
get the name but nothing in the component.

I have also had problems (clearly bugs) with predict.gam but in a
way difficult to reproduce: I have only had it with very large
calculations.

There are still many problems with S-PLUS 5.x it seems but I have
also recently had an encouraging experience: a large calculation
involving manipulating large objects within a loop was handled
reasonably well with S-PLUS 5.1 but on the same platform it
killed S-PLUS 3.4 and S-PLUS 2000 on a machine roughly as
powerful also became completely bogged down.  (Fortunately I
spotted a way to streamline the calculation a bit and now it runs
quite well on all three, but best on S-PLUS 5.1.)

You win some, you lose some...

Bill Venables.

messages.subject: Re: [S] Adding Constant Term in ARIMA model
messages.subject_clean: [S] Adding Constant Term in ARIMA model
messages.body_plain:
On Sat, 22 Jan 2000, Leyla Khoury wrote:

> I have tried fitting a time series model via the following command:
> 
> ARIMA.mle {x, model=list{order=c{1,1,0}}}
> 
> How do I add a constant term to this model so I can unite my output to
> SAS output?  This present model fitting procedure does not include a
> constant term.

Include it as a regression term (use xreg=).  _However_ that is a
differenced model, and it is unusual to have constant terms in differenced
models. (A constant term in X_t will make no difference at all.)
If you really want a constant in a differenced model, you will find it
easiest to difference the series manually.

messages.subject: [S] Summary: do.call("rbind", list)
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

Last week, I asked the following question:

> I have a list which is the result of by() on a dataframe. Each element
> of the list is a data frame with the same number of columns (13) and a
> variable number of lines (1 to 7). The length of the list is 1152. I
> want to turn this list into a data frame. I use do.call as follows, but
> it takes 25 minutes to complete !
>
> > length(Off2)
> [1] 1155
> > dim(Off2[[1]])
> [1]  7 13
> > dos.time(Off3 <- do.call("rbind", Off2))
> [1] 1499.66
>
> Is there a faster way to get the same result ?

I got 2 replies from Bert Gunter and Julian Taylor, using similar
methods:

Bert Gunter:
for(i in 1:length(Off2)) Off2[[i]] _ t(Off2[[i]])
matrix(unlist(Off2), ncol=13, byrow=T)

Julian Taylor:
t(matrix(unlist(sapply(Off2, function(el) t(el))), nrow =3)) 

Here is a small example:
> test <- list(A = data.frame(matrix(1:12, ncol = 3, byrow = T)), B = 
> data.frame(matrix(13:27, ncol
         = 3, byrow = T)))
> test2 <- do.call("rbind", test)
> test2
    X1.1 X1.2 X1.3 
A.1    1    2    3
A.2    4    5    6
A.3    7    8    9
A.4   10   11   12
B.1   13   14   15
B.2   16   17   18
B.3   19   20   21
B.4   22   23   24
B.5   25   26   27
> test2 <- test
> for(i in 1:length(test))
        test2[[i]] <- t(test[[i]])
> test2 <- matrix(unlist(test2), ncol = 3, byrow = T)
> test2
     [,1] [,2] [,3] 
[1,]    1    2    3
[2,]    4    5    6
[3,]    7    8    9
[4,]   10   11   12
[5,]   13   14   15
[6,]   16   17   18
[7,]   19   20   21
[8,]   22   23   24
[9,]   25   26   27
> test2 <- t(matrix(unlist(sapply(test, function(el)
t(el))), nrow = 3))
> test2
     [,1] [,2] [,3] 
[1,]    1    2    3
[2,]    4    5    6
[3,]    7    8    9
[4,]   10   11   12
[5,]   13   14   15
[6,]   16   17   18
[7,]   19   20   21
[8,]   22   23   24
[9,]   25   26   27

On my real data set, computing times are 1555.97, 85.59985 and 93.81006
for do.call, Bert's and Julian's solutions, respectively. The drawbacks
of Julian's and Bert's method are that all the columns are coerced to
character mode (I have both numerical and factor variables in my data
frame), and that column names are lost. However, this is easily managed
in a few subsequent steps.

Many thanks and best regards,

Renaud

On Mon, 24 Jan 2000, Stephanie MAHEVAS wrote:

> I do a simple linear model with n factors and each factor has
> respectively
> N(i) levels (i=1,..,n). The contrasts for fitting are default ones. To
> get the estimators' variance (to construct confidence intervals of each
> estimator' coefficient) I use the fonction vcov(lm.out) of
> library(MASS).
> The size of the variance-covariance matrix is
> [(1+(N(1)-1)+...+(N(n)-1))]*[(1+(N(1)-1)+...+(N(n)-1))] and not
> [(1+N(1)+...+N(n))]*[(1+N(1)+...+N(n))] as I would like ...!
> 
> WHY and anyone know how to get the variance of each coefficient
> (associated to each level factor)?

Take a look at the coefficient estimates. vcov is giving the variance
matrix of those, not what you think they should be. In a 2^n design there
are n coefficient estimates for the main effects, not 2n as your formula
says you are expecting.

I think you need to understand the way S fits linear models with factors
better: I assume you _have_ read the book whose software you are using?

messages.subject: Re: [S] on vcov()
messages.body_plain:
> 
> Dear s-plus users,
> 
> I do a simple linear model with n factors and each factor has
> respectively
> N(i) levels (i=3D1,..,n). The contrasts for fitting are default ones. To
> get the estimators' variance (to construct confidence intervals of each
> estimator' coefficient) I use the fonction vcov(lm.out) of
> library(MASS).
> The size of the variance-covariance matrix is
> [(1+(N(1)-1)+...+(N(n)-1))]*[(1+(N(1)-1)+...+(N(n)-1))] and not
> [(1+N(1)+...+N(n))]*[(1+N(1)+...+N(n))] as I would like ...!
> 
> WHY and anyone know how to get the variance of each coefficient
> (associated to each level factor)?
> 
> 
> thanks in advance.
> Stephanie

Dear Stephanie,

As Professor Ripley has already explained, the variance matrix
returned by vcov for the coefficient vector estimated in the
linear model.  For factor models these are a reduced set
corresponding to a (generally) non-redundant set of columns in
the model matrix.

If X (n x p) is a complete set of binary columns corresponding to
a p-level factor term (main effect) in a single classification
linear model, the non-redundant set of columns has the form XC,
where C (p x (p-1)) is the so-called "contrast matrix" for the
factor (and can be set in various ways).

Hence if b ((p-1) x 1) is the reduced set of coefficients for the
factor the complete set is g = Cb.  This relation shows how to
get the variance matrix for the full set as well.  For just one
main-effect term the computation would go as follows:

library(MASS)
fm <- lm(y ~ f, data)
b0 <- coef(fm)  
Vb0 <- vcov(fm)

C <- contrasts(data$f)
H <- rbind(c(1, rep(0, dim(C)[2])), cbind(0, C))
g0 <- H %*% b0
Vg0 <- H %*% V %*% t(H)

At this point g0 is the expanded coefficient vector and Vg0 is
the (1 + p) x (1 + p) variance matrix you were expecting.

You can see that if you have more than one term the calculation
is going to get rather tedious (mainly in calculating the matrix
I call H above), though it is easy enough to see how to do it, so
long as you only have main-effect terms.  If you have interaction
terms things get tricky as well as tedious.

There is a function available, dummy.coef() that will get you the
redundant coefficient vector (g0 above) but it will not get you
its variance matrix.  Writing a fully general function to produce
this expanded variance matrix is a programming exercise that
forces you to come to grips with the mysteries of contrast
matrices like nothing else.  The problem is that the calculation
is very tedious to program and in the end the expanded variance
matrix is rarely of any genuine statistical interest.

Bill Venables.

--

messages.subject: [S] Re: predict.discrim() bug
messages.body_plain:
Many thanks to Charla Lambert from Statsci for confirming that there is a 
bug in SPlus 2000's predict.discrim() function.  Using the period '.' 
syntax to define a discrim() object causes the predict.discrim() function 
to fail whenever the 'newdata=' argument is used.  The only known 
workaround at this time is to explicitly list all the dependent variables 
in the original call to discrim().  It isn't a perfect solution (especially 
with a large number of dependent variables), but at least it works.

Thanks Charla.
=====================

> If you find that some problems still 
> exist, stop S+, delete the
> __sum.txt, __sum4.txt, __.sum4i.txt files and

Whoa!  Never, ever, delete _data\___nonfi (3 underscores) or the similar
.Data/___nonfiles on Unix.  If you do you will lose the names of many of
your Splus datasets.  This file is used to store the names of Splus
objects whose names are not valid (or unambiguous) file names.  On
Windows these names include any with capital letters, some special characters,
or not fitting the "8.3" mold.

> The same is true for the _data directory 
> (obviously don't delete it!)

Yes, don't delete _data either, but if you delete _data\___nonfi
it is almost as bad.
